sections.content: ACCT 2010 covers the fundamentals of financial accounting: journal entries, adjusting entries, the accounting cycle, and preparing the main financial statements, then moving into topics like inventory, receivables, and long-term assets. The content itself is standard for an intro accounting course and isn’t conceptually difficult, but it builds on itself quickly, so falling behind on early topics like debits/credits and adjustments will hurt later. Some parts can feel repetitive or dry, but the material is practical and genuinely useful as a foundation for later finance and accounting courses. Overall, well-organized content that does what an intro course should.
sections.teaching: Prof. Kim is a great instructor for this course. He explains each topic step by step and walks through plenty of worked examples in class, which makes the mechanics much easier to understand than just reading the textbook. He’s clear, organized, and approachable, and he’s happy to answer questions during or after class. The in-class examples are the most valuable part of the course, so pay close attention and take good notes when he goes through them. Highly recommend taking ACCT 2010 with him if you have the choice.
sections.grading: The grade is mainly based on two exams, a midterm and a final, plus attendance/participation. The exams are heavily based on the examples covered in class, so if you’ve practiced those problems until you can do them on your own, you’ll be well prepared. There aren’t many surprises, but the questions still require accuracy and speed, and small mistakes in entries can cost you. Grading is fair overall, though with the curve you’ll need to do consistently well to land in the A range. Attendance is checked strictly and counts toward your grade, so don’t throw away easy marks by skipping.
sections.workload: The workload is reasonable for a 2000-level course. Outside of class, most of your effort will go into reviewing the lecture examples and practicing similar problems before the midterm and final. The biggest commitment is actually attendance since it’s strictly enforced, I’d strongly recommend going to every single class. Not only does it protect your grade, but missing a lecture means missing the examples the exams are built around, which makes catching up much harder. If you attend consistently and review regularly, the course is very manageable.

sections.content:
ACCT 2010 is the foundational financial accounting course for SB&M students (and others who need it). It focuses on the “language of business” — how economic transactions are recorded, summarised, and presented in the three main financial statements (balance sheet / statement of financial position, income statement, and statement of cash flows), plus basic analysis.Core topics usually include:
Accounting equation, double-entry system, and the full accounting cycle
Journal entries, T-accounts, trial balance, adjustments, and closing entries
Revenue recognition, receivables, inventory (including costing methods and COGS), PPE & depreciation, intangibles
Liabilities (current and long-term, including basic present-value concepts for bonds/notes)
Equity transactions
Statement of cash flows (especially the indirect method)
Basic financial statement analysis and some discussion of the discretionary nature of accounting / quality of earnings
The material is conceptual + applied. You need both to understand why something is recorded a certain way under GAAP principles and to be able to prepare the entries and statements correctly. Later chapters (inventory methods, adjustments, cash-flow statement, long-term debt) tend to be the steeper parts for many students. Real-company examples or annual-report discussions are often brought in to make the content less abstract. Overall the content is solid and practical — it gives a strong base for ACCT 2200 and later accounting or finance courses.
sections.teaching:
Teaching quality varies by instructor (the course is offered in multiple sections with different lecturers such as Steven Cheung, Wilbur Chen, Kelvin Mak, Tony Cho, Yue Zheng, etc.). Classes are typically twice a week and mix lecture, worked examples, and problem-solving discussion.
Most instructors post lecture notes/slides on Canvas and use the standard textbook (Libby, Libby & Hodge – Financial Accounting). Many sections emphasise in-class problem solving after introducing concepts. Some use polling or short memos for participation; others rely more on active discussion. Office hours and TAs are available, and students who prepare the pre-class reading and attempt practice problems usually find the lectures clearer.
The better sections explain the “why” behind the rules and walk through multi-step problems carefully. Weaker experiences tend to come from sections that move quickly through technical material or rely heavily on students self-studying the textbook. Because accounting builds sequentially, missing the logic of adjustments or the cash-flow statement early on makes later topics harder. Overall, teaching is generally competent-to-good if you attend regularly and engage with the examples.

Materials: He uses the publisher’s PowerPoint slides, which are more than sufficient. He also provides additional notes, but the main slides are all you really need.

sections.content: This is a fundamental introductory accounting course for business students. It covers basic financial accounting knowledge, including bookkeeping rules, journal entries, and simple financial statement preparation. The content is beginner-friendly and does not require prior accounting experience.
sections.teaching: The lectures are structured and systematic. Instructors explain core accounting concepts with clear examples and organize the course content logically. Tutorial sessions provide targeted exercise practice to help students consolidate knowledge and fix common mistakes. Teachers are responsive to questions and offer steady learning support throughout the semester.
sections.grading: The course grade is curved. It has midterm and final closed-book exams. The overall difficulty is moderate, but earning a high GPA is competitive due to grading scaling
sections.workload: The workload is relatively heavy and consistent throughout the semester. Students are required to finish weekly online homework every week. Each assignment takes around two to three hours to complete carefully. Since the tasks are ongoing and cannot be accumulated or skipped, this course requires stable time investment every week, which brings steady learning pressure.

sections.content: For students who have completed the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) Business, Accounting and Financial Studies (BAFS) curriculum—specifically the Accounting Module—transitioning to introductory university-level financial or managerial accounting often feels remarkably seamless. The rigorous foundational framework established during the DSE secondary years covers core concepts such as double-entry bookkeeping, adjusting entries, bank reconciliations, inventory valuation, and the preparation of comprehensive financial statements for various forms of business ownership. Consequently, learners who have deeply mastered these local high school principles possess an extraordinary advantage, frequently finding themselves well-equipped to secure top-tier grades like an A+ with relative ease during their initial higher education accounting assessments.
sections.teaching: he instructor's pedagogical approach was exceptionally effective, skillfully incorporating a diverse range of varied and dynamic questions throughout the session to make complex accounting concepts much easier to grasp. Rather than relying on repetitive drills, mixing up the problem types forced the class to analyze core principles from multiple angles, which successfully prevented rote memorization and deepened genuine understanding. This clever variety of real-world contexts and varying difficulty levels not only kept everyone actively engaged and thinking critically, but it also provided immediate opportunities to apply newly learned theories. Ultimately, this thoughtful blend of interactive teaching created a truly productive and supportive learning environment that made mastering the material feel both accessible and rewarding.
sections.grading: ofessor Wilbur is an absolute standout educator who truly sets his students up for success. Not only does he deliver engaging and accessible lectures, but his fair and reasonable grading policy—paired with straightforward, well-structured midterm and final exams—makes navigating a notoriously rigorous subject like accounting a genuinely rewarding experience.

Visual Aid: The use of PowerPoint presentations can serve as a valuable visual aid during lectures, highlighting key points, diagrams, and examples to enhance understanding.

Supplementary Material: In addition to lectures, PPTs can provide supplementary information, references, and resources for further exploration of topics.

Comprehensive Coverage: Textbook questions offer a comprehensive set of problems that reinforce learning and allow for practical application of theoretical concepts.
Diverse Difficulty Levels: These questions likely span various difficulty levels, catering to students with different levels of proficiency and providing a challenge for those seeking to deepen their understanding.
Self-Assessment Tool: Textbook questions can serve as a self-assessment tool, allowing students to gauge their comprehension and proficiency in different topic areas.
Extent of Content:

Abundance of Material: The presence of a substantial amount of content suggests that the course covers a wide range of topics in-depth, offering a thorough understanding of the subject matter.
Depth of Learning: The richness of content can facilitate a deeper dive into the subject, encouraging critical thinking and a comprehensive grasp of complex concepts.
Challenge and Reward: While the volume of content may pose a challenge in terms of workload, mastering this extensive material can significantly enhance your knowledge and skill set in the subject area.

sections.workload: In fact, overall, the amount of homework is not very large. It's almost one assignment every two weeks, and each assignment takes about one and a half hours. However, it is not enough to get high scores on homework, because this basic accounting course involves a large number of knowledge points that require in-depth understanding and repeated practice. Especially for students without an accounting background, it is still quite challenging to keep up at the beginning (many local students have learned this knowledge in high school and have a solid foundation). So I think the workload for self-study is quite heavy. It's best to preview before class and review thoroughly after class

sections.content: The materials are mostly copyied from the text book. However, real‑life example are not extensively explored. Its content is mostly progressive, you will have to stick to the course somehow, or it may be hard for you to understand the content in the later sections
sections.teaching: Kai is an genrally a kind prof. He is willing to answer lots of questions in the class. However, answering questions may sometimes affect the progress of courses. It's a little bit boring to take his course as he is just simply reading the power point and ask some general calculation example question.
sections.grading: Fair grading. The midterm exam was online and mostly seletive and fill in blank questiones. The final is a little bit harder cause we have practiced any paper written quiz before.
sections.workload: Worload is fair. There are several ongoing quizzes and weekly assignments throughout the term, you will be given way enough time to finish. You may need to take the assignments and quizs seriously cause some of the midterm questions may be extracted from your homework. Concepts build heavily on prior chapters. If you procrastinate and skip practice, you will struggle with subsequent topics. There are no essays or large‑scale projects. You may need to do a presentation before class to simply illustrate some contents to gain participation score.

sections.content:
The syllabus before the midterm basically matches with the BAFS DSE. It is extremely hard for non-BAFS students to catch up since the chapters are arranged in a weird position in my own opinion.

I think one of the chapters regarding adjusting entries is the hardest to catch up. This chapter requires students with no accounting foundation to categorize different items, and this consumes much effort. However, for some chapters after the final, the chapter summary actually clashes with the above chapter on adjusting entries to a large extent.

Generally speaking, I saw my friends getting almost full marks when they have studied accounting before. This is very frustrating for students like me.
sections.teaching:
Kelvin tends to use a lot of local Hong Kong shops as examples in classes, and even in Cantonese sometimes, which may be difficult for some non-local students to understand.

He also loves using many technical terms and specific accounting terms, before explaining them clearly before using them. It is easy for me to lose track of what he is talking about and soon I found myself falling behind and not understanding the following lecture materials even more.

He tends to do many examples using draft paper and youtube videos in the lesson, it may be beneficial to students who understand him, but not to students who found it confusing on all the calculations which he ASSUMES we should know .

His powerpoint only highlight the important point without explaining the rationale behind, so it is hard to understand without reading the materials in textbooks.

There are no lecture videos provided.
sections.grading:
Normal Grading. Only get mean but still manage to got a B.
Should note that the mean is quite high.

sections.workload:

Examples of last year's good works are also given.

sections.content: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to intermediate‑level investment knowledge. It systematically goes through modern portfolio theory, risk‑return relationship, CAPM asset‑pricing framework, equity valuation, bond pricing, market efficiency and basic performance evaluation for investment portfolios. The teaching materials closely align with the mainstream investment textbook. Apart from pure theoretical derivation, real‑world market cases are embedded into lectures, referencing historical market cycles and typical investor behaviour.
sections.teaching: The professor maintains a steady and logical teaching rhythm throughout the semester. Abstract financial theories and complex mathematical formulas are broken down step‑by‑step in class instead of simply throwing equations onto slides.
sections.grading: The overall grading scheme is exam‑oriented. Mid‑term examination and final examination occupy the dominant weight of the final course grade
sections.workload: For a standard 3‑credit undergraduate course, the total workload stays at a reasonable level. It is not a course you can pass by one‑night cramming before exams. Continuous weekly review is required to consolidate formulas and conceptual understanding.

sections.content:
1. Provides a solid and comprehensive introduction to financial accounting principles and the mechanics of financial reporting.

2. Starts with transaction analysis and the four fundamental financial statements (Balance Sheet, Income Statement, Cash Flows, and Stockholders’ Equity).  

3 Progresses methodically from core accounting cycles to more challenging topics toward the end of the term, such as bond accounting, inventory valuation, and cash flow statement preparation.  

4. Highly practical and structured, providing an essential foundation for any business or finance concentration.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Chao Tang structures lectures clearly and explains accounting logic from the ground up.

He uses interactive pop-up quizzes and review practical questions to reinforce key concepts in real time, and sometimes asks questions during the lecture to keep everyone engaged. But plz note that there is a participation component that students can earn by either answering or asking questions (after-class questions are also accepted). This participation point may also be earned from some pop-up quizzes.

Every lecture is packed with substance and really informative, so what you must notice is that you have to pay attention to the lecture; otherwise, you will lose.
sections.grading:
Assessment breakdown:
20% Homework (Connect)
5% Participation
25% Midterm Exam
50% Final Exam

Homework on McGraw-Hill Connect offers unlimited attempts (Prof is willing to take suggestions from students!!!), making a full 20% very attainable if you put in the effort.  

The participation score is an easy boost through in-class pop quizzes and actively asking questions.  

Exams carry heavy weight (75% combined), and the final is cumulative (although the first few chapters do not account for a large proportion). The final is much harder than the midterm. (I remember the average is around 48 out of 100) And keeping pace with the material is crucial, although the final is totally different from what we practice.

BUT!!! Prof is so nice in grading!!!

I got full mark in these two sections:
20% Homework
5% Participation

My exam scores are followed:
midterm 89/100
final 69/100

And I got A+!!!!
sections.workload:
The regular weekly workload is moderate (but initially, I spent 3-4 hours on each homework), consisting of Connect homework sets spread across the semester with generous two-week deadlines.  

No group projects or extensive written reports are required.  

The main workload involves practicing transaction problems and preparing for the cumulative midterm and final exams.  

Spending a few hours each week reviewing lecture slides and completing practice questions makes exam revision smooth and manageable.

sections.content: The materials are well‑structured for absolute beginners. Still, most examples are textbook‑based; real‑life complicated business cases are not extensively explored.
sections.teaching: Lectures are logically organised, yet the classroom atmosphere is fairly non‑interactive. There is little spontaneous class discussion. Students mostly passively receive knowledge. To master journal entries and accounting rules, relying only on in‑class lectures is insufficient; extra after‑class practice is indispensable.
sections.grading: Grading is based on quizzes and regular assignments. Rubrics are transparent. Be aware that arithmetic slips or improper journal‑entry formats can lead to harsh point deductions. Do not expect much partial credit once your core accounting logic goes wrong.
sections.workload: Workload is fair for an introductory accounting course. You have ongoing quizzes and weekly assignments throughout the term. Concepts build heavily on prior chapters. If you procrastinate and skip practice, you will struggle with subsequent topics. There are no essays or large‑scale projects.

sections.content: The course covers fundamental accounting concepts in a very structured and logical manner. It builds a solid base in financial principles, financial statements, and basic analysis. Even if you have no prior accounting background, the curriculum is easy to follow and connects well with real-world business scenarios.
sections.teaching: Prof. Kelvin is an incredible instructor. He brings immense energy to lectures, making accounting concepts far more engaging than expected. He breaks down complex rules using clear real-life examples and is extremely patient and approachable during office hours or after class when clarifying student questions.
sections.grading: The grading in this course is exceptionally good and generous. I failed on midterm and final but still get a grade that I am satisfied. Very fair and transparent grading scheme. The expectations for quizzes, assignments, and exams are clearly communicated upfront. As long as you review the lecture slides, complete the tutorial exercises, and understand the core principles, scoring well is very manageable.
sections.workload: Highly manageable and well-balanced throughout the semester. The weekly assignments and tutorial practices are directly aligned with exam materials, so keeping up weekly prevents any last-minute cramming during midterms or finals.

sections.content: ACCT2010 provides a foundational overview of financial accounting, concentrating on the preparation and analysis of corporate financial reports. The curriculum covers essential topics including the accounting cycle, financial statements, cash, receivables, and inventories . The course is designed to teach the fundamental principles of recording and communicating economic transactions.
sections.teaching: The course is delivered through a standard lecture format, often incorporating problem-solving and discussion sessions . Students are expected to supplement lectures by reading the textbook and completing practice problems, which are usually assigned through an online platform like Connect or My Accounting Lab . Many sections also utilize digital polling or in-class quizzes to encourage participation and gauge understanding .
sections.grading: The grading structure is heavily weighted toward exams, which can account for up to 75% of the final grade . The remaining points are typically split between assigned homework and class participation. While the weight of exams makes the course challenging, I found that the grading was very fair. As many reviews note, professors are often accessible outside of class for help, and there were opportunities for extra credit, such as completing study guides or assignments .
sections.workload: The workload for ACCT2010 is acceptable and manageable. The course requires consistent effort through weekly homework, reading, and regular practice problems to reinforce the material . Success depends on staying on top of the curriculum, which is a typical expectation for an introductory accounting course.

sections.content:
Principle of Accounting I
I. Course Objectives
Accounting is the language of business. In this course you will learn how to "speak" and
"read" this new language. The course is designed to provide an overview of financial
accounting so that, upon completion of the course, you will be able to read, interpret and
analyze corporate financial reports. In particular, you should:
1. Demonstrate a broad understanding of business functions and in-depth knowledge of
accounting.
a. Demonstrate a broad understanding of different business functions and domains to
formulate integrated solutions.
b. Demonstrate substantial knowledge of their business functions and domains to
formulate integrated solutions.
2. Develop a comprehensive and well-founded knowledge of financial accounting,
including
a. Understand the accounting categories: assets, liabilities, equity, revenues and
expenses;
b. Understand how an accounting system keeps track of information;
c. Understand how generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) influence what
is recorded in the books of an entity;
d. Prepare a balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement;
e. Read, interpret and analyse a set of financial statements.
2
3. Understand the role of financial accounting in the decision-making process of business
organizations. Apply financial accounting frameworks to business situations.
4. Be able to form critical judgment covering an ability to identify and define accounting
and business problems, apply analytical and quantitative techniques, make and justify
decisions;
5. Be effective in communication through collection, analysis and organization of
information and ideas and their clear transmission;
6. Demonstrate teamwork, independence and creativity including working, learning and
problem solving as a team and independently;
7. Demonstrate ethical and social understanding including a knowledge and respect of
ethics and ethical standards in accounting and an understanding of social and civic
responsibility

sections.content: This course covers the core building blocks of financial accounting journal entries, adjusting entries, financial statements, and how transactions flow through a business. It’s very practical and helps you understand what’s really behind income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements. Even if you’re not an accounting major, it’s super useful for business, finance, or econ students because it teaches you how to “read” a company through its numbers.

Tang Chao 教的很不错，我一个没咋系统学过会计的人，也能被教懂。上课节奏很好（一周一个chapter），但偶尔会因为怕讲不完，就开始提速，但可以课后要recording复盘。

他对会计学真的很热爱，本身数学专业出身，逻辑很清晰。课上非常欢迎同学的问题，也会很耐心的回答，很不错的一位教授。

学期中，会经常发匿名问卷，参考学生对于考试，作业评分方式，学习感受等方面的建议，会将结果搬到课上一起讨论并解释。这点我个人觉得很负责。

虽然是一位很好的教授，但不是一位很好的出卷人...哥们的final难如天！！！！！！！和课上的练习题完全不一样...但mid就还好，会相对更贴近练习题。

如果你觉得你的教授课上讲的不清楚，可以考虑来tang chao课堂坐坐。但要注意，每个教授的考纲都不一样。

TA Vincent 人很好，paper check会耐心解释错题，邮件也会及时回复。只是每次看到他那么深的黑眼圈，我都想就地给他搭个床，让他先补个觉。

- Basically write a two to three sentence summary of each class, but do not copy word for word and try to summarise in your own words. You can also ask questions in the memo as well. Each one should be ard 0.25% of course grade, I missed two
20% Assignments
- 10 in total on connect, at most each takes 2 hour but some take shorter like 15 minutes. you can do it unlimited times by checking your answers so try to complete it early as they’re a free 20%
25% Midterm
- easier than finals so try to get higher marks. beware of careless mistakes as they’ carry a lot of marks. explain everything well, the TA marks questions relatively leniently
Mean: 45.1/64, High: 64/64. I got 64/64
50% Final
- this is the hardest thing i’ve ever done, harder than accounting. Tony puts A LOT of emphasis on what-if scenarios, real life applications so it’s not actually heavy emphasis on accounting entries/calculations, but rather on the underlying concepts behind them, such as “what would happen if they did not do this method, what would happen if they violated this rule..” so UNDERSTAND THE CONCEPTS WELL. also, he has a part that carries ard 1/3 of the mark that is basically just you reading a REAL, corporate financial report (we got microsoft) and answering questions. so be familiar with them - there are some exercises available with real financial reports provided by tony.
Mean: 57/100, High 96.5/100, i got 89.5/100 which is fair.
Tony’s paper is harder by a lot than other sections so don’t be afraid if you don’t understand, everyone will get a lower marks anyways lol

Finals Course Mark ~94%, ended up with A+
quite good grading actually, probably due to lower cutoff and harder papers.
~85% for A-range
sections.workload:
not that bad

just be sure to complete assignments on time.
it’s ard 1 assignment/week so take your time and don’t be a deadline fighter lol, each takes only ard 1 hour anyway

for memos they’re a bit annoying but actually quite useful if you want to ask questions. try not to miss too much , i missed 2 but it’s fine everyone i know also missed ard 2 or above
just complete the memo after the class if you’re afraid you will forget it lol

For revision, the slides actually are not a lot of content, but you should really try out his exercises - they format is  pretty close (but easier) than the exam paper. as long as you do all of that getting a good grade should not be that hard.

sections.content: Basic accounting contents. Covers the four basic financial statements first, then examines each one in detail.
sections.teaching: Kai is always passionate about teaching and willing to answer questions after class—he is a very generous professor. However, I don’t think he teaches effectively. His lessons lack a clear logical structure, so I couldn’t follow his flow of thought. I’d say about 80% of the course came from my self-study.
sections.grading:
The grading seems fair. Since very few exam statistics were released, I’ll share my personal scores as a reference:

Participation: 3.33/5 (5%)
Homework: 19.9/20 (20%)
Mid-term: 160.79/180 (20%) with mean 75/180
Final: 132.75/150 (50%) with mean 90/150
Overall grade: ≈ 85 / 100 (A+)

Even this might look ideal, I would like to emphasize that I did spend A LOT of effort on studying this course by myself, as I had absolutely no prior accounting background.
sections.workload:
As mentioned in the Teaching section, the workload can be very heavy if you try to complete this course through self-study. I often had to reread the textbook multiple times. Kai assigns end-of-chapter questions online after each chapter. These questions are helpful for exam preparation, even though they don’t count toward your final grade.
In short, if you’re smart enough to skip self-study and practice (or you have studied accounting before), the workload will be light. Otherwise, this is a very demanding course.

sections.content:
I actually did some back accounting for a semester in high school, and I screwed up big time, so I consider myself someone with no background in accounting.

The content is actually not so bad. Have to say some concepts are hard to stand with, but just studying a little bit more and doing practice questions on Connect, you'll be fine.

Not so bad of an experience to have to say, compared to the time I did accounting in high school, I never dragged my body to Tony's class at least.

But details of content, read other posts (I threw all my acct knowledge out of the window right after my finals).
sections.teaching:
I read ustspace, and I also heard people saying he's not a good professor. I even have friends saying he's the worst.

Okay, have to say he's actually quite nice. I think he understands what he's talking about.
His English is decent, no accent, so very easy to listen to (no second-guessing)

He replies to emails almost immediately, usually within 2 hours.

Tony's a great guy overall.
sections.grading:
U need to rely on class participation, period. It's a very minor percentage on ur final final grade, but it's worth the participation. There are memos, so basically u submit what u learn from class after every single class, not so bad, just 3 sentences each??

I participated a lot in class because I knew my grades would be worse if I did not. Because of participation, I felt like Tony remembered my name already, so ig that help with my final grade? (He asks for names after u answer questions (even if it is wrong), he marks ur name down) So defo answer questions.

My friend had very similar grades to mine for both the final and the midterm, but they didn't participate in class (like answering questions). And so our final grade is different.

The midterm is easier than I thought.

The final is way harder than the sample papers + old exam papers. Preparing for the finals, I finished all textbook questions on McGraw-Hill, and it's COMPLETELY USELESS AT THE END.

I knew I screwed up big time the moment I stepped out of the exam hall, but it turned out that I was above the mean. So ig its okay la. I don't expect anything. I don't need good grades, I just want to graduate, that's it.

sections.teaching: On the good side, Prof. Dong uses the powerpoints from the textbook publisher, which is surprisingly actually not bad for self-study, and that his accent is fine even for a local Hong Kong student like me. However, despite his passion in class, the fact remains that even if you tried your best to listen, you walk away with very little knowledge gained that you can recall, leading you to feel confused and abandoned. Lectures are like a yapping session for Prof. Dong, and frankly of quite limited use. As someone who did not take BAFS in high school, I had to almost exclusively rely on self-studying with the heavy help of my friends in order to compensate for Prof. Dong's rather ineffectual teaching.
sections.grading:
Components Weights
In-class participation 5%
Homework 1 10%
Mid-term exam 25%
Homework 2 10%
Homework 3 Optional
Final exam 50%
Total 100%

The grading is alright, Prof. Dong is not as leng grade as some have led me into believing, but he is definitely not laan grade as well. I got an A from my 86.6% overall score, which was actually above my expectations. However, be prepared to lose marks in homework, where Prof. Dong is the only class that allows for only one single attempt per homework. Furthermore, you have to register on a first-come-first-serve basis for giving a presentation in order to get full participation mark. I was unable to do so and despite answering and asking questions very frequently in class, I only had 3.33/5 attendance. It is also worth mentioning that his mid-term was conducted face-to-face using an online platform, which was greatly annoying as it was a 9 am lecture.
sections.workload: Workload is manageable. Practice problem sets are useful but you do not need to submit them. Only best 2 out of 3 homework sets count, and each can be done in 1 hour. Moderate revision needed for exams.

Overall, the workload is perfectly acceptable compared to other 3-credit courses.

sections.content:
Hi there.

You might have seen a post in Threads where a CS guy decides to take a business course and got A+ by having a pretty low score. Well that person is me lol.

The only reason I'm writing this review is because the grading of this lecture is kinda insane, and since this is the first time Prof. Yue is teaching this, I think it's best to show what it's like taking her class.

I won't go over the details of the content, but overall it is a pretty good introduction to accounting.
sections.teaching:
9/10, but A regardless.

Her lesson is like an ASMR session, but in a good way. I was honestly expecting her to have heavy accent, but it was the complete opposite, the class is just super chill and her voice is very comfy. She also explains things slow but concrete, so even though sometimes I will read things ahead, it's nice to just listen again to see if she has anything to add.

One small critique: there was one time where I have a question on bad debt write offs, and we ended up talking for like 30 mins as she doesn't seem to understand my confusion. But honestly 99% this is fine as she usually responses pretty well to other students who doesn't have autism like me lol.
sections.grading:
Ngl this might be the best grading I have ever seen.

I'm not exactly sure how the course grading works, but I'm guessing that it's dependent on the instructor/lecture, so in terms of policy every class is different.

5 homework(best 4): 20%
Midterm: 25%
Final: 50%
Participation: 5%

My Score:
Homework: Full
Midterm: 95/100 (mean 72.7 sd 19.1)
Final: 72/100 (mean 50 sd 20)
Participation: 5/5

Overall Score and Grade: 84.5% and A+

So +1.1/1.2 sd is A+. wtf

I think I heard something about some A range might be reserved for non-business students, but that sounds unfair af so I don't think that's true.

One thing I want to mention is that participation is relative, where max score is the student who has the highest quantity of participation, and your score is the ratio between your quantity and their quantity, in addition to the quality of your participation (e.g. if that student raised their hands 16 times and you raised only twice, your score will be (5/16)*2; but if you raised some interesting questions, you might get one or two bonus points).

Sadly, we don't know how the quality is judged, but it will only plus instead of minus.

sections.content:
主要讲了会计学原理的基础内容
课程的syllabus我放在attachment里了（其实不是 但是可以通过这个知道学什么）具体是什么教材其实也不太清楚 讲的是GAAP原则 以为教材的用途只是用来做作业的 基本上没有看书 但是如果有不懂且老师的PowerPoint没有讲到的内容还是要看一下书的 尤其是chapter 5的内容 很多ratio老师根本没讲 但是还是考了 这个需要你自己去学一下
说要记attendance 但实际没有记录attendance 但是有记录participation 这个需要你在上课的时候回答问题或者提出问题 但是像我这个人比较shy 所以一学期只举手发言了3次 最后老师捞捞 给了两次 in-class quiz（一套卷子只要做对一道题就可以记一次participation 当然全做对也是一次）5次participation就可以拿满
In addition, 老师会发很多的MC question 和 additional practice 记得考试前要做 虽然考试的题型和难度和这些题目简直是天差地别 但是这些题能让你很好的对概念进行回顾
sections.teaching:
讲的很不错 基本上每堂座位都是坐满的 八十多个座位 81个学生好像 没有空座每节课（会有一些别的堂的过来学 因为讲的真的很好）
会把概念讲的很细 并且课上会有很多同学提问 这些问题有的也很能启发人思考 在课上也会用一些题目example来帮助你理解  很适合没有基础的同学从0开始学（当然完全从0开始的同学建议在bilibili YouTube上找一些课程先学一些基础 这样不至于手足无措）老师课下也会很耐心的答疑 中文和英语应该都可以吧（很愧疚没有怎么去答疑过 跟Deepseek老师交流的比较多）
而且Pro TANG真的很尊重学生 他会在几个时间点发问卷来询问学生对课程的意见和对考试形式和内容的想法 上课的时候会管纪律 课下如果能看到你的努力他还会给你发邮件鼓励你（本人期中考了98/100 他还发邮件表扬我来着/(ㄒoㄒ)/~~ 给本人哄成胚胎了）
sections.grading:
他好像没有公布这学期的participation和assignment和midterm和final之间的占比 但是我听我的朋友说她私下问教授 教授说主要看final
assignment答案可以无限次尝试无限次提交 所以说其实如果你不想学习甚至都可以直接交上去然后拍一下答案然后直接抄上去
midterm 考2小时 我并不觉得很难 就是作业的难度 但是会出现作业没有出现的MC question 15道MC 5道大题 教授说他会尽可能宽的给分 哪怕你中间有一个数算错了 他只会扣那一问的结果分 如果你过程没错 但是事实上是不是如此我并不清楚 因为我只错了道选择 我想如果你把平时的assignment都认真做了 且考前自己总结一下professor的slide的话我觉得85分以上是肯定能做到的 midterm mean是71 SD是13左右
final 考3个小时 具体的题型我放在attachment里了 题量很大要有心理准备做不完 我最后一道大题 因为没有好好审题的原因基本就没拿分 但是前面的题做的基本都全对了 最后score是 78/100 mean是51 SD是16 题目很新颖 考验的是你对所学知识在新环境下的理解与运用 会有一些类似但又不同的概念出现 要注意甄别
听说final 60分出头就可以给到A 那如果是真实的 那真的很好龟了 大家可以尝试去选一下Pro. TANG的课
sections.workload: 不算太小 如果你要把他发的所有内容全学全做 且你为了高分你需要保持一个每周的复习 但是对于SBM的学生来说 其实大一上并没有太多事 这点workload还是可以轻松应对的 当然 如果你很摆烂 你也可以像我说的方法一样把assignment如此混过去 且你不去上课也nobody cares

sections.content:
The course begins with the fundamentals such as understanding financial statements, journal entries, and the accounting cycle, before moving into topics like inventory, depreciation, bonds, and cash flow statements. The materials are well structured and follow the textbook closely. If you have studied BAFS before, the first few weeks will be quite easy, but even for complete beginners it is still manageable as long as you keep up with the lectures and exercises.

Some parts like adjusting entries and interpreting financial statements can be tricky at first, but Wilbur’s explanations in class are clear enough that you can catch up quickly. He does not test anything that was not covered in the lectures or slides, which makes studying more straightforward.
sections.teaching:
Wilbur is an excellent lecturer. His English is fluent, and his delivery is calm and well organized. He goes through concepts logically and uses simple examples to help you understand the reasoning behind each accounting step. He uses live polling questions during lectures to keep students engaged, and those questions also count toward participation marks. Even if you answer incorrectly, you still get credit for participation, which is nice.

He is approachable after class and answers questions directly. He is not the type to chat endlessly, but he gives clear and useful answers when you ask him something. His lessons are never rushed, and he rarely runs overtime.
sections.grading:
- Participation and polling: 5 percent
- Homework (Connect): 20 percent
- Midterm: 25 percent
- Final exam: 50 percent

The homework is completed on McGraw Hill Connect. It is open book and allows unlimited attempts, so with some effort you can easily earn full marks. It takes some time to get used to the platform, but once you do, it becomes a good way to review what you learned in class.

The midterm was quite challenging mainly because of the time limit. Many students could not finish all the questions, so Wilbur adjusted the marks afterward. The final exam was much more comfortable and focused on the main topics from lectures and homework. Overall, the grading felt fair, and the mean grade was on the generous side. I received an A, which reflected steady effort rather than memorization.
sections.workload: The workload is light to moderate. There is homework roughly every two weeks, participation through polling each class, one midterm, and one final. There are no group projects or presentations, and you do not have to read beyond the textbook and slides. If you keep up with lectures and spend a little time practicing before the exams, you should do well without much stress.

sections.grading:
Achieving high grades in this course is quite challenging.  

To secure an A range (90-100), you need to perform exceptionally well, as the grading is strict and competitive. This requires a deep understanding of the material and consistent accuracy in your work.  
A B range (70-90) is more achievable for most students, but it still requires effort and a solid grasp of the concepts.  

The course does not grade on a curve, so your performance is evaluated strictly based on the quality of your submissions and exams. Even small mistakes can significantly impact your final grade, so attention to detail and thorough preparation are crucial.
sections.workload:
The workload in this course is manageable and well-structured, but it requires consistent effort to stay on top of everything. Here's a detailed breakdown:  

There is one assignment per week, which is not overly time-consuming but does require a good understanding of the lecture material. The assignments are practical and directly related to the concepts taught in class, so keeping up with lectures is essential to complete them efficiently.  

The midterm covers a significant portion of the course material, so preparation is key. While the workload for the midterm isn't overwhelming, you’ll need to allocate enough time to review concepts, practice problems, and ensure you have a solid grasp of the basics.  

The final exam is cumulative and requires a deeper understanding of the entire course. Though the preparation workload is higher compared to the assignments and midterm, it is manageable if you’ve been consistent throughout the semester.

sections.content: The content he produces is consistently exceptional, standing out for its remarkable depth and clarity. He possesses a unique talent for distilling complex subjects into digestible, engaging, and highly actionable insights. Beyond the sheer quality of the information, his presentation is flawless—his delivery is both authentic and charismatic, making learning not just easy but genuinely enjoyable. It’s this powerful combination of expert-level knowledge, meticulous research, and relatable communication that makes him an invaluable resource. I never miss a post, as each one delivers significant value and leaves me feeling more informed and inspired.
sections.teaching: He is undoubtedly one of the most exceptional professors I have ever had the privilege of learning from. His mastery of the subject matter is profound, but his true gift lies in his ability to translate complex concepts into clear, accessible, and logical explanations. He never makes students feel rushed or inadequate; his patience is truly remarkable. He cultivates an environment where no question is too small, and his helpful, thoughtful responses demonstrate a genuine investment in every student's understanding and success. He is the gold standard for what an educator should be.
sections.grading: While the tests and exams are notoriously challenging, designed to truly probe our understanding of the material, the grading itself is surprisingly decent and fair. It’s clear the professor isn't trying to trick us or weed students out arbitrarily. Instead, the difficulty seems intended to push us to master the subject, and the grading rubric generously acknowledges the effort and knowledge we do demonstrate. This balance makes earning a good grade feel like a genuine accomplishment, reflecting real comprehension rather than just the ability to memorize simple facts.
sections.workload: The course workload is very reasonable and streamlined, primarily consisting of some periodic homework assignments delivered through Canvas. There isn't an overwhelming amount of busywork; the focus seems to be on self-study and understanding the core concepts rather than completing endless tasks. This approach provides enough practice to stay engaged with the material without being burdensome, ultimately placing the responsibility on the student to prepare for the challenging but fairly graded exams. It's a refreshingly straightforward structure.

sections.content:
Content
First off, don’t worry if you’re a non-accounting high school student. Even if you didn’t study BAFS, like me, you can manage this course. It covers essential accounting concepts, including the four financial statements and their components.
sections.teaching:
Teaching
Now, let me share my thoughts on the teaching aspect.not the worst teacher; his English is proficient, and he does teach us valuable content. However, I found his approach quite rude, which negatively impacted the learning environment.

often comes off as impatient and defensive. For instance, when I asked him why my classwork was marked down by 30%, he sent a lengthy message criticizing me for not reading the guidelines. The issue stemmed from a mix-up with my name order on Zoom, which was not clearly stated in the rules. I felt his reaction was excessive, especially since my grade was affected.

Moreover, he tends to lose patience when students ask deeper questions, which can make the classroom feel intimidating. I often hesitate to reach out to him for clarification, as he seems to favor students who interrupt him and ask questions without hesitation.

Additionally, he sometimes assigns classwork that isn’t covered in lectures, which feels unfair to those of us without prior knowledge. His sudden quizzes at the end of classes also add to the anxiety, but that might just be my personal issue!

Finally, I recommend previewing the slides before lectures. assumes we already understand the basics and skips over fundamental concepts. For example, he won’t explain what a 'write-off' is before diving into journal entry steps.
sections.grading:
I ended up with an A- in this course. We had 8 classworks, 3 homework assignments, and a final assessment with 50 questions to complete in 60 minutes. The grading policy felt unclear, and he didn’t provide much feedback after the finals.

Also, I advise against asking  about grading policies, whether in person or via email, as he tends to respond harshly.
sections.workload:
The workload isn’t too heavy. Most assignments are done on MH Connect, which includes access to our e-book and online tasks. There are no mandatory readings, just a few open-book online assignments during class. Homework assignments take more time, especially the one on inventory systems, which took me about 3-4 hours to complete.

Overall, while the course content is manageable, the teaching style and grading policies could use improvement.

sections.content:
To do really well in this course, you need a good grip on the basics of accounting. The best way to get there is by regularly practicing problems and going over your notes and slides. You can try just memorizing how to do journal entries and other routines—that might get you by—but putting in real effort is key, especially if you haven’t taken accounting before.

The class covers all the important stuff: how to put together financial statements (like the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Statement of Shareholders’ Equity, and Cash Flow Statement), writing journal entries, and handling accounting for stuff like equipment and inventory. It’s a lot like what you’d see in the first half of the HKDSE Accounting exam.

If you’ve done accounting before, you’ll probably find this pretty easy. If you’re totally new to it, it might feel tough at first, but don’t worry—you can definitely catch up and do well if you stick with it.
sections.teaching:
The professor's a super clear lecturer who uses lots of real-life examples to show how accounting actually works in the business world, which makes the class way more interesting.

He's really chill and fair with grading. Even if you get a problem wrong, he gives partial credit for showing your work. A pro tip: make sure to go to his lectures because he often drops hints about the homework.

His teaching style is "big picture first" (top-down), so don't stress if you're lost at the beginning of a topic—he always circles back to the details. He's also really approachable and happy to answer any question.

Plus, he's just a nice, humble guy who shares cool stories and life advice, making his class about more than just accounting. Definitely take a class with him if you can!
sections.grading:
The midterm is really easy—it's basically exactly like the problems he does in class. Pretty much everyone aces it, so scoring 100 is totally doable.

But watch out for the final! It's super long and hard on purpose to spread out the grades. You’ll definitely need to study up for this one.

Since almost everyone does really well in this class, the average is sky-high. That means you can’t afford to make silly little mistakes on the homework or exams if you want a top grade. Every point counts!
sections.workload: The course has a very light workload with only three assignments, and they're easy to get a full score on. There are no group projects or other major tasks, so you can just focus your energy on studying for the midterm and final exam.

sections.content:
This course covered the fundamentals of basic financial accounting, providing a comprehensive introduction to key concepts and practical applications. The topics were organized as follows:

1. Course Outline & Overview of Financial Accounting: An introduction to the scope, importance, and foundational principles of financial accounting.  
2. Investing, Financing Decisions & Balance Sheet: Examination of how investment and financing activities affect the company’s financial position, with a focus on understanding the balance sheet.  
3. Operating Decisions & Income Statement: Analysis of operating activities and their impact on company profitability, emphasizing the income statement.  
4. Adjustments, Financial Statements & Quality of Earnings: Discussion on adjusting entries, preparation of complete financial statements, and assessment of earnings quality.  
5. Sales Revenue; Receivables & Cash: Understanding revenue recognition, accounts receivable, and cash management concepts.  
6. Cost of Goods Sold & Inventory: Exploration of inventory valuation methods and cost of goods sold calculation.  
7. Property, Plant & Equipment (PPE): Accounting for long-term tangible assets, including acquisition, depreciation, and disposal.  
8. Current Liabilities: Overview of short-term financial obligations and their accounting treatment.  
9. Long-term Debts & Present Value Applications: Treatment of long-term borrowings and the use of present value concepts in accounting.  
10-11. Owners’ Equity: Examination of equity components, stock transactions, and dividend distributions.  
12. Statement of Cash Flows: Preparation and analysis of cash flow statements to assess liquidity and financial health.  
13. Course Revision: Comprehensive review of all topics to consolidate understanding and prepare for examinations.
sections.teaching: The professor made a clear effort to communicate as clearly as possible and always took time to answer students’ questions at the end of each class. He was mindful that many of us did not have a background in accounting, so he frequently checked in to see if anyone had questions or needed clarification. This was very helpful for students new to the subject. However, at times his voice could be somewhat monotonous, which made it a little challenging for me to maintain full attention throughout the lectures. Both the midterm and final exams were quite difficult for me, and I often felt that the time provided was insufficient to complete them comfortably.
sections.grading: Since I did not study accounting in high school, I found the course quite challenging and did not perform as well as I hoped. I don’t believe this was due to the professor’s teaching style; in fact, he seemed understanding and supportive throughout the course. The only exception was the final exam, which I thought was particularly tough. Overall, I got the impression that the professor did his best to help students like me pass the course, which I appreciated.
sections.workload: The workload was moderate—neither too light nor overwhelmingly heavy. There were several homework assignments, each consisting of 10 to 12 questions. While the number of questions seemed a bit much at first glance, the level of difficulty was reasonable and manageable. During class, we were also required to participate by answering multiple-choice questions or short questions to earn participation marks, which helped keep us engaged without adding too much extra work.

sections.content: Understanding accounting principles is interesting for me as a student who has no prior knowledge in business and finance, in other words, accounting has a low barrier for entry and teaches you the macro view and core goals of business; but boring when we have to do all the conventional and repeated practices, in my own opinion. As a non-BAFS student, I found the course content aligning with BAFS content, yet covering new concepts like bonds and shareholder statements. Overall it adds depth without overwhelming students.
sections.teaching: Cho Tony teaches the old subject of Accounting in a fresh and youthful manner. His energy and humor create an engaging classroom environment. He simplifies challenging topics effectively, using clear explanations and relevant real-world examples. Cho Tony did a great job by patiently answering every question that students submitted after class. He gives out useful tips in the revision sessions before midterms and finals, and gives practice papers for us to prepare. He likes asking tricky questions in exams, such as not accounting for the transaction when transaction date exceeds accounting period, whether or not we should account for that transaction for FOB shipping contract details... (save for later use!!).
sections.grading: ACCT2010 is a weird course where the sessions for different professors take different papers for midterms and finals. In my experience, his exams were noticeably easier than those of other professors (such as Tang Chao), which positively impacted grades. However, achieving a competitive grade requires near-perfect homework scores, as assignments carry some significant weight. He set goals about his expectations on midterms and finals, if class behaves too good in midterms, he will make the finals harder, and vice versa
sections.workload: The workload is moderate and manageable. Assignments are frequent but straightforward, particularly when tackled with a study partner. For HW, it is a must to strive for a perfect score for your grade to be competitive. As a weird course where the sessions for different professors have different assignments, this professor is a nice choice to be swapped.

sections.teaching:
My experience in Tony Cho’s accounting class has been anything but effective. Despite his apparent expertise in the subject, his teaching style creates significant challenges for students due to his rapid pace, overly complex explanations, and lack of engagement. These issues make learning accounting more difficult than it needs to be.

One of the most significant issues with Professor Cho’s teaching is how fast he moves through the material. He seems to assume that everyone in the class is already familiar with the concepts he’s teaching, which leaves many students struggling to keep up. Instead of taking the time to explain foundational concepts thoroughly, he rushes through slides and examples, barely pausing to check if students understand. As a result, many of us feel lost during his lectures, and the pace makes it nearly impossible to take proper notes or ask questions. For a subject like accounting, where precision and understanding are critical, this rapid approach is counterproductive.

Another major flaw in Professor Cho’s teaching is his tendency to make even simple topics seem unnecessarily difficult. Instead of breaking down concepts into smaller, manageable parts, he often uses overly technical jargon or confusing examples that complicate the learning process. Many students rely on clear, straightforward explanations to build their confidence in accounting, but his teaching style instead leaves us feeling frustrated and inadequate. When students ask for clarification, his responses are often vague or overly complicated, adding to our confusion rather than resolving it.

Lastly, Professor Cho’s lectures suffer from a lack of energy and engagement. His monotone voice and repetitive teaching style make it hard to stay focused during class. Accounting is already a challenging subject to make exciting, but a professor’s enthusiasm can make a significant difference in keeping students motivated. Unfortunately, Professor Cho’s lack of effort to engage with his students or make the material interesting only adds to the difficulty of his class. Many students dread attending his lectures because they know they will leave feeling more confused than when they walked in.

The combination of Professor Cho’s rapid teaching pace, overly complex explanations, and disengaging demeanor has created a class environment that hinders learning instead of fostering it. Many students, including myself, find ourselves spending hours outside of class trying to piece together what we should have learned during his lectures. While some level of self-study is expected in any course, the burden placed on students in this class is far beyond reasonable.

Professor Cho teaches with the assumption that everyone has a solid understanding of the basics of accounting, which is not reasonable.

sections.content:
Taking this accounting course has been a challenging yet eye-opening experience. The content is inherently complex, requiring a deep understanding of financial principles, intricate calculations, and strict adherence to rules and standards. The course demands consistent effort and attention to detail, as even minor mistakes can lead to significant misunderstandings.

While the instructor is knowledgeable and provides clear explanations, the difficulty of the material itself makes it easy to fall behind. Concepts such as financial statements, accrual accounting, and cost allocation require not just memorization but also strong analytical skills to apply them correctly in different scenarios. The pace of the course can feel overwhelming, especially when new topics build on previously covered material that needs to be thoroughly understood.

That said, the instructor provides helpful resources and is willing to clarify concepts during office hours, but staying on top of readings, practice problems, and seeking help when needed is crucial for success. Overall, accounting is a challenging subject that requires dedication and perseverance, and students should be prepared for a steep learning curve.
sections.teaching:
I honestly enjoyed this accounting class because of the professor. He’s super chill and creates a comfortable learning environment that makes even the hardest content feel a bit more manageable. His teaching style is straightforward and easy to follow, and he has a way of breaking down complex accounting concepts into more digestible pieces without making students feel overwhelmed.

What really stands out about him is how approachable and understanding he is. He’s always open to questions and takes the time to make sure everyone is on the same page, whether it’s through in-class explanations or during office hours. He doesn’t just teach the material—he makes an effort to connect with students and ensure they actually understand it, not just memorize formulas
sections.grading:
The professor is also very transparent about grading criteria, outlining expectations clearly from the start. He provides helpful feedback on assignments and tests, so you know exactly where you stand and what areas you need to improve. Plus, he’s always willing to discuss grades and offer advice on how to boost your performance, whether it’s through office hours or additional resources.

Another great thing is that there are extra credit opportunities and makeup options, which show that the professor genuinely wants students to succeed. He understands that everyone has different learning paces and gives ample chances to catch up or improve if you're willing to put in the effort.

Overall, the grading in this course is fair and encourages consistent effort rather than just cramming for exams. If you stay engaged and take advantage of the opportunities provided, you’ll have a solid chance to do well.
sections.workload:
The professor doesn't overwhelm students with excessive homework, and the workload is well-paced throughout the semester. Assignments and quizzes are spaced out reasonably, giving students enough time to complete them without feeling overloaded.

However, while the workload itself isn’t too heavy, studying for the course takes a lot of effort.

The content is well designed and it could lay a solid foundation for ACCT learning.
However, from my perspective, the content is a little bit unfriendly for NON-BAFS students and you might find it hard to learn through initial learning.

sections.content:
[I took this course as a non-SBM SENG student for my minor requirement, so anyone non-SBM/never took a business related course may find it useful]

Book: Libby, Libby, and Hodge. Financial Accounting

1. Financial statements and business decisions.
2. Investing and financing decisions and the accounting system.
3. Operating decisions and the accounting system.
4. Adjustments, financial statements, and the closing process.
5. Communicating and analyzing accounting information.
6. Reporting and interpreting Sales Revenue, Receivables, and Cash.
7. Reporting and interpreting Cost of Goods Sold and Inventory.
8. Reporting and interpreting Property, Plant, and Equipment; Intangibles; and
Natural Resources.
9. Reporting and interpreting Liabilities.
10. Reporting and interpreting Bond Securities.
11. Reporting and interpreting Stockholders’ Equity.
12. Cash flow statement.
13. Analyzing financial statements.

Chapter titles from the book, chapter 13 was to be covered if we had enough time, which we did. Gives you very basic idea about how accounting works for simple manufacturing based firms. You'd learn enough accounting to learn to produce and analyze reports for simple firms. But I think the content is WAY TOO MUCH.
sections.teaching: While others may not like his laid back approach, I REALLY liked him. People talked about how they did not attend his lectures since attendance wasn't required, but I went regardless. He speaks in an articulate manner, has a decent English accent (compared to other profs in my experience), and would answer questions in and after class. He made accounting really interesting to me as an engineering student who never did an accounting class. If its the first time for you doing accounting I'd highly recommend you try prof Kai. He is young, smart and very friendly. 10/10 prof
sections.grading:
Can't really complain. Grading distribution is as follows (for his section only, may vary between other professors):

Class Participation: 5%
Homework 1: 15%
Homework 2: 15%
Homework 3: 15%
Final: 50%

The homeworks were take-away home exams you had 10-14 days to finish after being published. For every 4 chapters we had one homework covering all the contents, and the homework is to be completed on the McGnaw Hill portal, the one you get access to upon purchasing the book (yeah you need to buy the e-book license)

Kai would transfer one of the homework weights towards the final exam weightage, whichever is the highest.

For finals:
Mean: 103.91/180
Median: 107.5/180
LQ: 84.5
UD: 127.5

I got 106, which yielded me a B (I did get full score for participation though since I was active in and out of class, and homeworks usually yielded high, near 95% mean scores).
sections.workload: Workload was pretty manageable. Again, he did not require attendance so it didnt feel like I was being shoved against my will to sit through a 9 am class twice every week. No midterms as well. If you did regular reading (both his slides and book) you'd be more than prepared. But not having midterms meant ALL 13 CHAPTERS would show up in your finals in their entirety, so ggs. That's my only complaint. Only times you'd feel a bit burdened would be around the time you have to submit the homeworks and the final exams. Huge amount of reading and content must be covered if you want to do well. But compared to other engineering courses (*cough*COMP2012*cough) ACCT 2010 was not bad at all.

sections.content:
Chapter 1-4, the macro part of the course, the main structure of financial statements, some key concepts, the process of accounting, and some ratios. Also, you will learn how to write T-accounts, entries, ledgers, etc. The above is what I can think of after 2 weeks from when we finished the final, which I think is important. For details, see others’ plz.
Chapter 6-12, Prof. Mak skipped chap5 and didn’t introduce chap10 bond due to the limited time. Here you will have a detailed look at each account. The last chapter, chap12, is about the cash flow statement, with a focus on the indirect method.
In the beginning, I thought this course meaningless. Even if I quite understood this so-called “language of business” by Kelvin is making the business world more efficient, I did not think learning this language was meaningful to me or humans overall. But gradually I found it interesting to understand the accounting system and gained insights into the business world more or less, which is also what Kelvin said he wanted actually to teach us. The course is beneficial and interesting if you try to understand it. However, indeed, it is quite difficult to understand it fully at least for me. To achieve this, my suggestion will be to carefully go through all the pages in the textbook before classes and review them again before homework and exams.
sections.teaching: Many students especially those without an accounting background like me may feel extremely confused about Kelvin’s teaching in the very first few weeks. I guess it is because Kelvin loves foreshadowing much content that will be learned later and introducing many examples, scenarios, and knowledge beyond the syllabus in one go. Well, personally speaking, it is absolutely worthwhile to struggle to figure all things out and stick to his classes. You will see Kelvin’s 良苦用心. Getting exposure to the knowledge ahead enables you to better understand it in the subsequent learning in a natural way. He will teach you something interesting that is not included in the textbook, but can be found in FINA2303! Kelvin is a real teacher who really cares whether you can learn something useful and understand all the things well. He encourages us to raise questions and is open to answering them. And sometimes he is quite humorous (only pretended to be serious and strict in exams :) It was he who aroused my interest a little little bit in business and even made me want to major in accounting, but he told us not to for some reason, so.
sections.grading:
Good grade. I did some calculations by the means I learned in ISOM2500 and it turned out that my score on the final was around the 90th percentile. (midterm too lazy to calculate, I guess similar) So, I estimated it would give me an A, but it is in fact, an A+. The fault tolerance is fairly high since I had one question that I could not even get fully done at last in both midterm and final but still not bad. Thank you, Kelvin!
For reference: Homework full*25%+midterm (50.5/60)*25%+final (85.5/100)*50%=88.7917 overall. For detailed statistics see the attachment.
Homework (25%, from best 5 in 7 or 6) Can have infinite time and 3 attempts each week so everyone can score nearly full marks. BUT! I was too stupid and found we could actually, know which answers were wrongly done in the previous attempts late in the second last homework. ^_^ So I wasted much time trying to score full marks with one single attempt before. I know few people will be as stupid as me but just to remind you here, in case.
Midterm (25%) Multiple-choice (forget how many, 20?) including both conceptual ones and numerical ones. 2 or 3 questions (forget exactly again, sorry) asking you to calculate some ratios, explain something, or write some entries. 1 hour is very tight for these but they are not that hard. You should remember all ratios, how to write general entries and adj entries, etc. because no cheat sheet is allowed.
Final (50%) 40 Multiple-choice and 5 questions. This course is difficult for beginners without any accounting background. There is a steep learning curve where you have to pick up the whole system and be adept at it within three months.
This is why I truly recommend you to spend time doing practise questions every week, cuz only paying attention in class is not enough to handle homework and exams.
Prof Tang drowned us with a ton of practise exercises so if you want to perform good in this course, do them!!!

As for the final exam, to an Acct beginner like me, it was very difficult. The questions are closer to real-life accounting than those hypothetical short questions we've been practising on. The paper is nothing like the question types provided in the sample paper, which prof did remind us about.
So I would recommend y'll to look for past papers to prep for the final if possible, not only doing materials provided by prof.

1. Prof Tang speaks English with almost no Chinese accent.
(top reason why you should choose his lecture)

(as he mentioned in the first lesson, he's been teaching this course for a long time)
He's well prepared before every lesson with practise questions to review last lesson's teaching and his delivery in lessons is fluent and coherent without much stuttering.

3. Prof Tang values student feedback.
He had set a total of 4 surveys throughout the course to ask for our feedback ,like whether he is teaching too fast, how is the difficulty of the mid-term exam and is cheat sheet preferred in the final exam, etc. You can always give your honest opinion to him and he will adjust accordingly.

4. Prof actively provide assistance. He is patient to answer the line of questions after lessons and he would provide study guide to help us prepare for mid-term and final exams. The study guide summarizes everything you need to master in each chapter and he would specify the type of questions that would appear on the exam paper so you would know whic chapter to spend time on. It is inevitable for SBM students or people who are minoring in business to take this course as it is one of the business core courses. For those who want to acquire some business knowledge, this is one of the most basic yet important courses as accounting is the foundation of business.

Speaking of difficulties, it is quite challenging for me as students with and without accounting background are in the same class and i need to catch up the progress. From my perspective, it is really compacted and face paced. In the final which is cumulative, we need to revise for nearly 800 pages of the textbook and never-ending slides.

But if you work hard, particularly in Wilbur’s class, i can guarantee you your grades will not be bad. Do the exercises in the textbook at the end of each chapter as the homework is similar if not exact to them. Also, most questions from the Quizzes and exam are from the textbook but with little to none alternation. Therefore, if you do most of those questions, the effort you have put in this course will definitely pay off.

As mentioned above, no need to worry about getting extra sources as the exercises in the textbook is more than enough. Solution manuals are given by Wilbur.

Rumours has it that ACCT2010 is one of the easiest and best grading course on HKUST business core. So don’t be afraid of taking this course. Also, note that this course’s grade is used in choosing the accounting major in MSE, so it will be quite competitive.
sections.teaching:
If you decide to choose ACCT2010 as your course in your next semester, I would recommend Wilbur.

About Wilbur’s teaching, he has good delivery and very understandable English. One of the main reason that i show up in Wilbur’s class is his accent and how efficiently he conveys knowledge about accounting to us.

The second reason is he is flexible and truly cares about students. Throughout the semester, there  sometimes will be a few assignments crammed together. You can tell that to Wilbur and politely ask for postponing the deadlines of the accounting assignments. Also, most people did bad in a quiz, he would simple gives everyone marks.

In the beginning of this course, i thought it was going to be a disaster as i did not have any source to familiarise myself for the quiz. Under the request of some students, Wilbur gave the solution manual of the textbook which really helped me. If you encounter any difficulties or want to trash talk with him, Wilbur is always here to provide you assistance.

The reason why i gave him a B but not an A is because I fell asleep in most of the classes and did not pay attention. I studied most of the syllabus by myself and participated in the Q&A session, asking Wilbur some questions.

Quiz:
The midterm is replaced by 2 Quizzes with each one covering 4 chapters. The questions are quite challenging but you can find most of them in the chapter exercises which number and data changed, so if you are hardworking, those 20% are not hard to score. Also those quizzes are inclass.

In the first Quiz, there was basically one super long question and tells you to produce financial statements, Journal entries with deferrals and accruals, and closing entries. Make sure you memorised the format.
Mean: 25.4/40
Me: 40/40

In the second Quiz, it has a few short questions which involves bank reconciliation with format given, FIFO & LIFO, and ratios, and gives you accounting frauds and requires you to state which accounting principles they have violated.
Mean: 34.9/50
Me: 41/50

Final exam (3 hours)
The main focus is the chapters that have not been covered in the quizzes. The short questions involve statement of cash flows, bonds securities, liabilities and stocks. The MCQs basically cover everything. The questions could be found in the chapter exercises also.
Mean: 74.1/100
Me: 98/100
(PS somebody i know got around 90 in final and ate a B+)

Participation:
It is based on completion on the polling of the menti slides he used in each lesson. Just attend all lessons and answer all of them and you are guaranteed to earn 5%

Assignments:
You have 3 attempts in each assignment and most people get 100% in them, make sure to do them and you will get 25%.

Overall:A+
sections.workload:
The course suggested us to spend at least 10 hours a week on this course. Personally, i spent about 7-12 hours to fully understand and do most of the exercises for a single chapter as a student without accounting background.

About the homework, it is tedious. There were 5 assignments on connect, about 1 per week, and it took me about 4 hours in average to finish one. However, those questions are from the chapter exercises with the data and number changed. So if you are lazy like me, just follow the solution manual and follow the step, replace the number in the manual with those in the assignment, and you can get the answer. I should have found it earlier :(

Another reason the workload is quite high is the Quizzes. The midterm is replaced with 2 Quizzes and each quiz covered around 4 chapters.  Every Quizz, i just gave up half of the last chapters that the quiz required as i simply did not have enough time for the revision. In the final, i only got 4 hours left to finish the last chapter. It was not the professor’s problem, but simply the course is quite challenging to be handled for students with no accounting background.  

There is 5% participation and you need to attend all the lectures and answer menti questions. It is horrible for me as a student who doesn't love attending lectures. I usually sat in the last row and fell into the limbo of awake and asleep.

sections.content: Decent content for the course in general, great for an entry course to accounting, but each professor has their own variations of the coursework and syllabus, with CHO, Tony's being the worst (by a long shot).
sections.teaching:
Absolutely terrible, the professor is wayyyy too fast paced, by the time most other professors were done with first few basic chapters, we were done with 70% of the course syllabus. He teaches with the assumption that you have decent prior knowledge about accounting when most students studying this course are taking it as an intro course and can't keep up. Personally, I don't even think his teaching could be considered good even if you had prior knowledge, most complex concepts aren't explained in-depth as needed.
His lecture slides are in general helpful, but some of his own questions are answered wrong in his slides so they aren't always reliable. Some of his slides are also quite vague, they barely mention a new concept, show a random graph and move on.
He gives a review exercise before mids and finals and each time some of the answers were wrong so it only created more confusion.
His section feels like a completely different course altogether, if you need to take this course or get pre-enrolled into it, drop it immediately or switch sections if you can, literally any other section would be better for your mental health.
sections.grading: Grading for mids was fair, homework grading can be quite rigid. Attendance is checked through a memo that you have to submit after each class in which you write about what you learned in that class, which is a bit annoying and unnecessary (especially because it makes attending classes pointless, just fill in the memo and you get your attendance marks).
sections.workload:
Too much for an entry-level accounting course (just for this professor, it's fine for the other sections). Homeworks are unnecessarily long, and you need at least a few hours to attempt each one (there's gonna be at least a dozen homework exercises).
Overall occupies a lot of time for no reason, if you plan to take this course, take any other professor to maintain your own sanity.

Our class(all except one was a business student, most people are taking this to fulfill business minor requirement) was taught by Deng Jin.

sections.teaching: Pretty good. Prof. Shieh can explain things quite clearly. He likes to give examples and go through the fundmentals behind economic behaviors. If you follow him carefully, take notes, go over course materials and do adequate exercises, it is not difficult to learn financial accounting well and understand the basic logic behind it. He encourages students to raise questions in class and will answer them very patiently.
sections.grading:
I heard that his grading was bad and was a bit worried. Actually his grading is quite fair.
5% for participation
10% for in-class group exercises
10% for in-class quizzes
35% for midterm
45% for final
may be inaccurate!
Raising thoughtful questions and trying to answer his problems actively help. He will write down participating students' name on the whiteboard and ask the TA to record participation.

If you want to learn financial accounting well and earn a good grade, you must have to put a lot of effort. Doing exercise, reviewing, reflecting...So the workload is a bit heavy but worth it.
