sections.teaching:
I really like how Tang Chao makes his PPT readable and easy to understand. He also uploads recordings of the classes in Canvas, so you can always rewatch the videos to study. He incorporates daily life examples as well to help us understand the application of accounting on a daily basis !

For Tang Chao himself, he is very friendly and has no accent. It is easy to listen and understand him ( especially if you are an international student ). He is very open to questions in class and the class is quite interactive.

However, his tests are soo hard. Especially the final test, most of the questions are things that we've never encountered before. The results are also not released.
sections.grading:
Curved grading.

He counts activeness, so you gotta be active in class in order to get extra points. Although it is not that big ( 5% if I'm not mistaken ), but it can change your score from C to C+. So I think it is worth trying.

My final grade is B-, and I think it's good enough because I struggled to do the final exam.
sections.workload:
There are homework every 2 weeks that you can access from the text book. The homework is not easy, I had a hard time doing it. However, it really helps you to grasp the materials and most of the questions in the exam are similar to the homework. So, I just think of it as a practice for the exam.

There are no projects or group discussions. Thus, I think it isn't that time-consuming in terms of the workload, but you must use that time to study because the materials aren't easy!!

sections.content:
Accounting is the language of business. In this course you will learn how to "speak" and
"read" this new language. The course is designed to provide an overview of financial
accounting so that, upon completion of the course, you will be able to read, interpret and
analyze corporate financial reports. In particular, you should:
1. Demonstrate a broad understanding of business functions and in-depth knowledge of
accounting.
a. Demonstrate a broad understanding of different business functions and domains to
formulate integrated solutions.
b. Demonstrate substantial knowledge of their business functions and domains to
formulate integrated solutions.
2. Develop a comprehensive and well-founded knowledge of financial accounting,
including
a. Understand the accounting categories: assets, liabilities, equity, revenues and
expenses;
b. Understand how an accounting system keeps track of information;
c. Understand how generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) influence what
is recorded in the books of an entity;
d. Prepare a balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement;
e. Read, interpret and analyse a set of financial statements.
2
3. Understand the role of financial accounting in the decision-making process of business
organizations. Apply financial accounting frameworks to business situations.
4. Be able to form critical judgment covering an ability to identify and define accounting
and business problems, apply analytical and quantitative techniques, make and justify
decisions;
5. Be effective in communication through collection, analysis and organization of
information and ideas and their clear transmission;
6. Demonstrate teamwork, independence and creativity including working, learning and
problem solving as a team and independently;
7. Demonstrate ethical and social understanding including a knowledge and respect of
ethics and ethical standards in accounting and an understanding of social and civic
responsibility

sections.content:
There's nothing much to say about the contents of this course. Basic stuff including an overall description of financial accounting, then a closer look into assets, liabilities and shareholder's equity. You would also learn journal entry and other techniques
that would help you to make all these statements. The topics which Tony went through this semester is listed below.
Ch1 Introduction; Overview of corporate financial reporting
Ch2 The financial Statements
Ch3 The measurement fundamentals of financial accounting
Ch4 Accounting Equation, Journal Entries and Adjustment Entries
Ch6 Cash and Accounts Receivables
Ch7 Merchandise Inventory and Cost of Goods Sold
Ch9 Long-Term Assets
Ch10 Current Liabilities and Contingencies
Ch11 Long-Term Liabilities: Notes, Bonds and Leases
Ch12 Shareholder's Equity
Ch14 Statement of Cash Flows
The contents on the syllabus seemed to be rather friendly, but those who learnt accounting would then agree with me that these basic concepts and their application is already too tough for beginners. However, I would also tell you that these basic knowledge is quite helpful in your life or possibly in your career, and learning this course is a little more then just getting a good grade.
sections.teaching:
Tony haven't taught courses below 4000 for many years (I checked his personal page to learn this), and it is reasonable to assume that he haven't taught UG students for the same length of time. He is a good instructor, and his teaching style is appealing, however sometimes he just forgets that we are just a bunch of UG students that have zero experience in accounting. He would skip explaining some "fundamental" concepts and focus on those that he believed to be confusing and needs extra attention. He also focused on real-life application, provided sufficient examples in class and taught us to read financial statements of companies like Apple and GOME. These contents would also appear in mid-term and final exams.
In conclusion, Tony is a great teacher, but if you really want to get an A in his course, refer to Youtube and spend some extra time on financial accounting for your own good.

As for myself, I was very active that Tony remembered my name so I guess my participation is full marks.
Quizzes and exercises are easy to get a pretty high score so no worries about these.

sections.workload:

However, due to the nature of this course, and your own desire to get a good grade, you would find yourself spending extra time watching online resources and struggling to finish past papers. You would also face those peers who seem to be working all the time and giving you huge amount of pressure.
I, as a student from mainland China, must state that involution is the origin of all the workload.

sections.workload:
Class Preparation: Read the slides before coming to the class. Class preparation is essential for
earning the class participation marks.
2. Reading after the Class: The lectures give you a guidance of the key concepts in every chapter. You
should read the relevant chapter after class and make sure you can understand the materials in the
textbook. Exams will be based on the key concepts discussed in the lectures and the related
details in the textbook.
3. Practice Problems: A set of textbook problems from each chapter are recommended for your
practice. Practice problems aim to improve your understanding of and familiarity with the topics
lectured in class. However, the amount of practice problems assigned is very minimal. You are
strongly encouraged to do additional practice while preparing for the examinations. The solutions to
practice problems at the end of each chapter will be posted on the course website.
4. Quizzes and final exams: Quiz 1 will cover chapters 1 to 4; Quiz 2 will cover chapters 6 to 8 and
the time value of money. The final exam will cover everything we have discussed in the class. This
course does not cover chapters 5 and 13 of the textbook.

sections.content:
This course focuses on Generally Accepted Accounting Principle and teaches you basic stuffs in accounting. After fully absorbing the course material, you are expected to:
1. know basic professional ethics of accounting
2. book journal entries (80% of this course, in different situations)
3. post the journal entries to a ledger
4. find useful information from 4 types of basic financial statements
5. construct simple financial statements (BS, IS, and Statement of Cash Flows)
The difficulty of the items above is ascending.

I am a Mainland Gaokao student and I have no background in any business subjects. From my perspective, the course is newbie friendly and intellectually rewarding enough.
sections.teaching: Professor Tang explains each concept very clearly and always provides student with concrete cases. He answers students' questions patiently and listens to students' advice. He also sends warm encouraging messages to students after the midterm. Generally speaking, he is a really nice and respectable professor.
sections.grading:
Grading Scheme:
Attendance (iPRS): 5%
Homework (unlimited attempts): 20%
Midterm (easy): 25%
Final (difficult like hell): 50%

!!! Get mentally prepared for the final !!!
The MCs are long and need your clear knowledge with some intuition.
For long questions, Professor Tang will tell his students in advance what is going to be tested. You REALLY need to pay GREAT ATTENTION to this and do much exercise.
There is also a module of questions defined by Professor Tang called "challenging question". This semester, the challenging questions are heavily associated with T-accounts, which is a great surprise to me and makes me feel like dying in the exam venue.  

I won't be surprised in the future if I hear someone in LG-1 cafeteria saying that "Oh, Professor Tang put a WHOLE K-10 report into the appendix of his final paper this year."

The grade is actually very good. I got full marks in homework, 98/100 in midterm, 4/5 (maybe) in attendance. The score of the final is not released. According to my estimation, I may get 40-70%, but I still got an A. Thank you Professor Tang!

sections.content:
Introductory accounting course for accounting beginners.
Textbook used: Financial Accounting, Robert Libby, 11e.
If you have studied BAFS in high school, you have already learnt most of the 'concepts' in the course.
I use the word 'concept' rather than knowledge because some of the knowledge is different from what we learned in HKDSE. For example, the methods of calculating allowance of doubtful accounts differ from those taught in HKDSE. There are also new depreciation methods such as the double-declining balance method. New topics related to bond, share, dividend and statement of cash flow are taught.
  Once again, if you have studied BAFS in high school, things will be easy.

Accounting was created by people to simplify existing problems in business. As long as you understand that it is nothing more than a set of rules made by people and start to think within these rules, the class becomes easy.

Most accounting is just remembering/knowing things, which is why it becomes boring quickly.
sections.teaching:
In comparison to other professors, Kelvin would spend more time for the first few chapters to make sure that people with no accounting background would understand the topics.

While other groups were writing a midterm for the first 7 chapters, we only did it for the first 4 chapters.

Kelvin would always stay after class to discuss any questions related to accounting.
sections.grading:
30% - Take-home assignment exercise (the best 4 submissions counted towards the total assessment)
20% - Mid-term exam
50% - Final exam period of Fall Term

Midterm mean: 44.5/60
Final mean: not yet published

Midterm was really easy with no challenging questions.

Kelvin has mentioned that he has not seen a significant difference between people who studied accounting in high school and people who started in college, and I agree.
sections.workload:
Kelvin provides Practice problems for every chapter we are studying. Although he does not emphasize doing them during the class, and would not grade them, I strongly suggest you do them all. The midterm questions were somewhat similar.

The final was disproportionally confusing compared to the Midterm. Some questions were hard to understand, but none were super challenging.

You can finish each problem set after each chapter in 1-2h, and every assignment takes around 1-2h.

sections.content:
The content of the course can be a little boring or confusing if you aren't into the financial accounting side of business management.   A lot of the content revolves around transaction analysis, different financial statements, and how to record transactions.

The course and content is pain for students who never did accounting before, because they cover a lot in a very short time.
sections.teaching:
Wilbur is quite good at presenting topics of this course and his presentation slides are quite tidy.  However, I recommend using the online textbook video explanations for revision, I don't really fully understand topics just from lectures and slides.  

He speaks fluently, but sometimes too quickly for some students unfamiliar with accounting.  

The TA is also very helpful, he replies to emails relatively quickly and provides answers and example questions.
sections.grading:
Participation 5%.  For Wilbur's class, you only need to answer Menti meter questions during lectures.  You don't need to get it right, just make sure you attempt every question for the 5%.   

Homework 20%.  Assignments on the CONNECT online textbook.  

Midterm 25%
Final 50%

Pass is 55%

There are 2 types of people in this class, those who learned accounting before and get 70-90%, and those who never took it and get below the mean.  So PLS study each topic well or u might die.
sections.workload: The workload is pretty good for this class.  Only one homework assignment every 2 weeks.  The homework itself might take some time to do if you aren't too familiar with how to record transactions and fill out sheets and it can get a bit frustrating sometimes.  However, you do get unlimited attempts for every assignment.  Prof Wilbur is also willing to extend deadlines for students with problems accessing homework online.

Also, he doesn't care if you attend classes or not so long that you finish all your work and secure yourself a decent grade in his course.

sections.content:
It covers the four basic financial statements in modern accounting—the income statement, the balance sheet, the statement of stockholder's equity and the statement of cash flows.

In terms of the difficulty of content, I wouldn't say the content, per se, is difficult. In fact, it's quite manageable for most. What's hard for most students is the tricky aspects when multiple new contents come together. However, following the course and doing all the work in a timely manner will get you there. (although bear in mind TANG Chao's finals are notoriously a killer... don't be fooled by the relatively easier midterms)

Another thing I liked about this course is that it does not test your memorization skills. Whenever they tested theory (in midterms or finals), they would make the answer obvious, in the sense that you didn't need to memorize exact or word-for-word phrases in preparation. They focus more on testing your understanding of how accounting actually works.

If you have DSE BAFS background, you definitely have a competitive edge, as I've seen my friends with no accounting background struggle a bit more with this course than those with some type of accounting background in high school.
sections.teaching:
Professor TANG, Chao was extremely nice and helpful throughout the course and was always willing to stay behind and answer your questions.

He also conducts multiple surveys (I believe one was in the beginning, one in the middle and one at the end) to get a better sense of how his students are feeling about the content/ workload/ pace etc. I liked this about him, as it shows that he takes student feedback into consideration.

One thing I really liked about this course is how he would make us do practice questions at the beginning of the lecture "recapping" things we learnt last class, as well as a few questions at the end of the lecture, helping us consolidate our understanding of what we learnt for that class.

There's no prominent accent or anything, and his teaching is easy to follow.
sections.grading:
In terms of the grade composition:

Homework - 25%
Mid-Term - 30%
Final Exam - 40%
Participation/ Attendance - 5%

↑ for the "participation" marks, you just have to answer his Zoom polls. You don't need to get the questions correct, but just answer them all!

For the homework, you have unlimited tries, so although some of them may be time-consuming I think it really consolidates your understanding and isn't all bad!
sections.workload:
Out of all the aspects, the workload would have to be the biggest downside of this course as it is simply the truth that practice makes perfect! You could do the bare minimum, in which case you can't expect high grades.

In my opinion, though, it's not a matter of this course but just accounting in general which requires much practice for you to be able to tackle different exam questions in a timed environment.

It also depends on how self-motivated you are, as I know different students spend vastly different amounts of time preparing for this course (and usually that correlates with your final grade in this course as well...)

75% of my grade was about 97%

Every week there is online homework and a very short in-class quiz that relates to the homework and the chapter of the week. Although the homework takes a bit of time, it really helps with understanding and is an easy A assignment as you have more than one attempt.

I recommend studying for the quizzes by doing the homework and the optional concept checks on the online platform where homework is posted. Additionally, attendance is only required on quiz days but you should attend class because she explains concepts well and answers all questions. Attending all the classes helps show initiative, but if you have a complete grasp of material Professor Chen’s class would mean you don’t have to attend as much.

He also used Excel frequently to explain the concepts, maybe its more straightforward, but for me, some steps maybe skipped in Excel, and some details may be missed (the things he typed in Excel were different in different sessions) , so personally I didnt really like this. However, he gave us in-class exercise to do sometimes and walked around the lecture hall to check our answer, which definitely helped us !

In general, he is a really friendly professor, who is really to answer students' questions. sections.content: The content of the first half of this course is similar to that in DSE BAFS(accounting), including the preparation of financial statements and adjusting entries. The second half is about long-term financing, including the issuance of bonds and stocks, which are not covered in DSE. However, some of these topics are covered in FINA1303 (so I highly recommend you to take FINA1303 at the same time).
sections.teaching:
Professor Chen adopted a blended-learning mode, where we watched the lecture videos filmed by herself before we attended classes and she would just do some review on the content during lessons. There would be a chapter quiz once a week/every 1.5 weeks, all of which were held in class.

To me, Prof. Chen is just super nice and passionate. You can literally feel her passion in teaching when you watch her lecture videos, and that she was able to condense all the key concepts in her lecture videos in a clear and concise manner (it only took me around 15-20 mins to finish watching her lecture videos for every chapter). Whenever I encountered difficulty in completing the assignments, I would send an email to her and she would reply in a timely manner with detailed examples and explanations given (even during the weekend!), making sure that I didn't have any misconceptions.
sections.grading:
There are a total of 11 chapters, with 8 chapter quizzes (4 questions each) where each of them constitutes 2% of your total grade and 2 comprehensive quizzes where each of them constitutes 7% of your total grade. The questions for the 2% quizzes are really basic (for students with an accounting background) while the 7% quizzes require more thinking and are pretty challenging.
There are 10 assignments that you have to complete individually, one per chapter and none for the last chapter. Each assignment constitutes 2% of your total grade and you get 2 attempts for each of them. Even though you screwed up in your first attempt, you do not have to worry as aforementioned, you may email her and she would teach you patiently.
There is also a group exercise for each chapter, where you have to read news articles and finish the questions assigned by Prof. Chen. Those questions are easy in general, some of them are thought-provoking though. The 10 group exercises constitute 22% of your total grade, and you would secure the score as long as you submit them on time.
Besides, there would be participation scores awarded which constitute 3% of your total grade. You can either raise questions on the discussion board in Canvas or answer her questions during lessons and take a selfie with her after the lesson ends to earn a participation mark. You only have to do these four times in order to be awarded full marks for participation.
Lastly, the final exam constitutes 25% of your total grade. There are 3 sections in the final exam paper, namely basic, intermediate and advanced levels. The full mark of the final exam was 148. While she said that the basic level questions were similar to that in those 2% quizzes, I felt like those so-called "basic level questions" were already more difficult than those in the 7% quizzes, and I am pretty sure you just can't imagine how hard the questions in the rest of the exam paper could be. What made me find the exam exceptionally difficult was that each question required extremely complicated calculations, yet no marks would be awarded if your final answer was wrong.
For your reference, I got full marks in all quizzes and assignments except for one 2% quiz. I also secured the 22% from group assignments as well as the 3% from participation. The score for the final exam was not released "in order to avoid unnecessary panic" as quoted from Prof. Chen. While I bet I did not score any higher than 30% in the final exam, I managed to get an A+ at last. Therefore, my suggestion would be to try your best to secure the 75% from quizzes, assignments, group exercises, as well as participation so that you can have some sort of "safety net".
sections.workload: While the workload was relatively large compared with other professors/courses, I would say that it was manageable (may be biased because I learned accounting in high school and I took FINA1303 in the same semester so I didn't have to spend so much time understanding most of the concepts). Also, Prof. Chen's arrangement makes you do revision for the content of each chapter every week, and you would find that a lot of time could be saved when you study for the final exam. Moreover, it was the workload that allowed me to get a good grade. Therefore, I actually love the way Prof. Chen designed this course

Kelvin’s teaching is interesting and practical but lots of times, it is out of the syllabus and makes students confusing. He likes to share some practical issues with us. For example, he always talks about franchise business which is unrelated to our syllabus. But this kind of knowledge is useful if you want to study deeply in accounting.

You must attend his lecture to know what is going on. Because his ppt is too concise. You won't be able to know what does he means by just reading the ppt. During our lesson, Kelvin just shows a ppt slide and does a lot of explanations. We have to write down the main points! He speaks very fast and seldom repeats. You have to write very very very fast to catch up his speed.

If you have no accounting background like me, it is very hard to understand what is going on. For example, in the first few lectures, Kelvin will assume we all know some accounting terms e.g. Credit and debit, fair value, historical cost, residuals. I don't know what is going on... He speaks very fast with lots of accounting terms. I can just stare at him. I want to cry when I was looking at those T accounts. However, if you pay enough effort, you can tackle it! I watch his lecture video many times and read the textbook. Actually, the textbook is better than the professor. I learn everything from the textbook before I attend the lecture. So I could catch up and understand the accounting issues. Therefore! Don't give up!

One time, he chatted with us and answered our questions until 8 p.m. So he is very responsible! The best handsome professor in UST!

He always asks questions during the lessons. These are easy questions. You can just shout out the answers. if no one answers, Kelvin will answer them by himself but he is so poor! So remember to respond to his questions!

sections.content:
An introductory course for accounting that covers the 4 financial statements and how to record different items under different circumstances. I do not like how rigid and strict accounting is so I did not find the course very captivating. The concepts are not difficult to memorize and understand individually but there is a lot to remember in total.

For details on the topics covered, please refer to the attached course syllabus.

My overall comments for this course are as follows: You can safely get a lot of points from group exercises and assignments (also quizzes but depends on how much effort you pay). You should choose her if you only want to secure a decent score. You shouldn't choose her if you want to have a higher chance of getting a high grade (Prof Chen says only a few students got in A-range in her class)
Most suitable for people who have studied accounting before (economics does NOT help at all).
sections.teaching:
Professor Chen adopts a blended-learning teaching arrangement, where students watch pre-recorded videos for each chapter (around 15-20 mins) as pre-study at home and she will go through some questions and examples in lessons (which are not compulsory as she claims). It is an acceptable arrangement. However, I think she does not explain enough concepts to students. If you do not have an accounting background (i.e. haven't studied accounting before in high school or somewhere else), this course may be a little tough for you to get on given the rapid pace (details in the 'WORKLOAD" section)

She utilizes the discussion section of Canvas well by setting up a discussion chat for questions to be answered on or before each lesson. She usually answers by directly replying to the Canvas discussion chat. She is responsive and tries her best to leave no questions unanswered (unless she forgot and you have to remind her).

One good thing about Prof. Chen's class is that she gives us a lot of additional exercises to complete (completely optional) so we have plenty of exercises. There is also a Smart Book Reading on McGraw-Hill Connect which can show you the respective concept covered in the question you did from the textbook.

Lessons with quizzes are compulsory. She sets a passcode to access the online quiz so you must be present to get it. Although lessons without quizzes are optional, something troublesome is that Zoom recordings need to be requested if you want to watch them. I attended all lessons so it didn't affect me.

The TA (LEE, Sapere KK) only appeared in one of the pre-study videos and in an announcement or two so we never actually met her. I have no comment for this TA since she is next to non-existent.
sections.grading:
Interactions and discussions 3%
In-class group exercises (10 sessions) 22%
In-class quizzes (10 quizzes) 30%
Homework assignments (10 assignments) 20%
Final exam 25%

The best part about the grading is that the daily marks take up a large proportion so you can claim a lot of marks here. The final exam takes up a lot less but it really should. Read on to know why.

Interactions and discussions refer to answering questions during lessons and asking questions on Canvas discussion or in lessons. You get the full score by doing any of the above for 4 times.

The content in group exercises is usually 50% in-syllabus and 50% out-syllabus and an article may have to be read. Professor Chen gives you the full mark as long as you finish it and submit it on time (mistakes will not deduct your score).

Quizzes are done on a paid ebook platform called McGraw-Hill Connect (everyone must purchase it for ACCT2010) in closed-book format. Single-chapter quizzes usually consist of 4 MC and/or 'select all appropriate choices' questions. The quiz questions are claimed to be the 'basic' level and they are indeed mostly simple. Comprehensive quizzes have the same format but may include 'numerical response' questions (i.e. filling in the value of a computational question).

Homework assignments are also done on McGraw-Hill Connect. Questions are usually filling in the blanks of financial statements according to the info given. 2 attempts are given so it is in your best interests to ask for all correct computational methods before your final attempt (everyone has the same questions but different numerical data).

The final exam... is NOTHING LIKE THE usual quizzes and homework. It is split into 3 parts: basic, intermediate, and advanced. 'Basic' was 30 marks, 'Intermediate' was 76 marks, and 'Advanced' was 42 marks. The intermediate part was already too overwhelming for us since what we usually do are the basic-level questions. We were allowed to bring in 8-pages of cheat sheets, but even with them the final exam is a guaranteed FAIL. The same also occurs to students who get full marks in the quizzes. I hope Prof. Chen keeps her word and only allocates 25% to the final exam.

There is a choice for us to shift at most 7% of our quiz scores to the final exam. Still, the decision has to be made before the final exam. After experiencing the final exam, I can say with certainty that you mustn't do that since your final may well be a disaster.

All in all, the grading is decent if the final exam does not take up any more than 25%, so I will give it a B.

The results for the final exam are unknown (in her latest announcement about our grade, she said 'The final exam grades will not be released in order to avoid unnecessary panic') but I know I got a B+ for my grade. You are recommended to refer to the Word file I attached which is the 'final exam' announcement from Prof. Chen to get a better idea of the grading.

sections.teaching:
Sorry for the upcoming rambling guys, I just want to tell you how awful he is!!!!!

Dennis is not bad in teaching. He does teach us something, and his English is proficient compared to other prof. Rather, I often found Dennis being utterly rude, which really affected the learning atmosphere. Many people in this page praised Dennis for being a great teacher and you'll probably think I'm just a 打手 who got a bad grade (though merely an A-). So allow me to explain.

Dennis Chan is an impatient, strict and stubborn man who gets all-defensive easily, which often put me and my classmates off. One time I asked about why my classwork was deducted by 30% in a neutral manner, & he responded with a very long message condemning me about not reading the guidelines... To be frank, I did not intentionally put my full name in wrong order, and that you didn't write in the rules that the order is to be put right, but merely 'full name as stated in student ID card'. Both of us have the responsibility to fix the issue, and besides, it is my grading that is affected, but not yours. There is no reason for him to be so angry :)

Second, he loses patience easily when you ask him more questions in depth, and it often feels like he is angry with students. After such undesirable experience with him, I just feel frightened whenever I ask him something via email. (Ironically, he only smiles and nods with know-it-all non-locals who interrupts in the middle of his sentence and raise questions.) I really wanted to learn more about the accounting mechanics, but unfortunately Dennis is not the prof that I should ask for.

Third, he sometimes puts up classwork that are not even mentioned in class (he mentioned compensation expenses, but not the whole procedure). This is totally unfair to those who are willing to learn but don't have related knowledge, compared to those who had learnt such in high school ! By the way, his policy of having sudden quizzes at the end of some classes without prior notice makes me really nervous. But I guess it's just my problem lol

Lastly, remember to preview the slides before lectures because he assumes us to already know something about the concepts and thus will not explain the basic ideas. For instance, he won't tell you what a 'write-off' is, and he just jumps right into the journal entry steps, assuming that you already know it. He only kept giving us trivia that are only useful when you get the gist of the content/ want to get into accounting major.

The grading policy is super intransparent. He gives no details after the finals.

sections.grading:
Grading Scheme:

Class Participation 6%
- Class participation is based on:
- a. attendance record;
- b. whether the webcam is turned on;
- c. frequency & quality of questions you raise in class;
- d. frequency and quality of your responses to questions raised by the instructor or other fellow
students;
- e. participation in group discussion;
- f. Any behaviour that causes disturbances to the class (negative)

Homework 24%
- 11 homework assignments
- You will be graded based on the best 8 homework exercises out of 11.
- You get three attempts for each assignment and the attempt with the highest score will be graded.

Test 1 10%
- Chapters 1-4

Test 2 15%
- Chapters 6-8

Test 3 15%
- Chapters 9-11

Final exam 30%
- Chapters 1-12

You will need to buy the Connect code to complete the homework exercise and tests.

The final exam was a written exam.
sections.workload:
Light but frequent workload.
1 HW assignment every week, 1 test every 3 weeks.

The assignments are not difficult but they are frustrating to get right. There are also MANY questions in each HW.

Many non-graded practices are available.

(Just to clarify, I did not forget to grade the four categories, this course simply gets a solid C from me. It's better than a pass, but it's just not a particularly good course as well.)

sections.grading:
Grading Scheme:
25% In-class discussions and exercises
-10 sessions, full marks as long as you attended the session)

30% In-class quizzes
-10 quizzes, 8 of them are in form of simple MC questions (usually 3) on a specific chapter (each takes up 2% of total weight), 2 of them are comprehensive quiz with MCs and short questions with numerical answer (they cover Chaps.1-4 and 6-8 respectively, and each takes up 7% of total weight).

20% Homework assignments
-10 assignments, each corresponds to one chapter, and the marks of the assignments will be converted to the final mark. The allowed attempt for the assignment will be reduce after few chapters, so read the instruction carefully. The assignments are done on Connect platform and the questions are from the textbooks and professor provides answers to the question in textbook as well (but be careful that the numbers will be different). Professor will also teach how to do the assignments in the Q&A sessions, and on the discussion corner in Canvas.

25% Final exam
Final exam will be significantly harder than the previous quiz, but it's still MCs and numerical answers.

It is possible to "transfer" not more than 9% weight (that is, four small quiz, or one small quiz and one comprehensive quiz) in in-class quizzes to final exam (i.e. use the mark in final exam to replace the mark in quiz(zes) when calculating the final score) before the final exam, but DO NOT do so unless you missed a quiz and got 0 or you completely messed up the quiz, as the final exam is significantly harder than the quiz, so transferring the weight will just lower your final score in most circumstances.

sections.workload:
Not sure how he grades participation, but I attended all of his lectures and turned my camera on for most of them as well as asked questions in the Q&A sessions. I didn't speak up much in class so I guess it wasn't a large factor in grading.

I did preview and make notes for the whole semester, it is quite time-consuming for students without financial knowledge to understand everything from scratch, but building a good foundation in the early few weeks helps you immensely in grasping more difficult concepts.

The homework is quite difficult. You get three tries in each assignment and it counts the last try as your final mark. For most of the assignments I finished in 1-2.5 hours, but sometimes it took me 3-4 hours depending on my level of understanding.

The practice questions are useful in helping you understand concepts used in the homework as they are similar. As quizzes and exams have similar questions to the homework, make sure you understand the questions in homework and also do all if not most practice questions.

Only the final exam requires you to write on paper. It is divided into two parts, part one on connect and part two on canvas. Part two is written and only examines the last few chapters. You are also allowed to bring in a cheat sheet. Pay attention for the long questions in the practice questions, it is likely that the final contains questions requiring you to answer in the same pattern.

sections.teaching: She is a really nice professor cuz she would answer all sorts of questions and is very efficient when it comes to replying to emails. You can tell that she puts in the effort to make the course more fun and interesting. I don't know if this is the case for everyone but for me, all of Prof Chen's ACCT2010 courses are in blended-learning mode, which means that you have to watch some pre-recorded videos before the lecture. Instead of teaching the actually course content during the lecture, we are suppose to watch all the videos before class (in which I totally didn't do). Prof Chen will answer your questions and give you a brief summary about last week's stuff. If you ever have any questions, just ask her. She uses her email like Whatsapp.
sections.grading:
Before I go into detail, my dumbass got a mere C+ in this course. I did DSE, but I did not study BAFS. I think that if you DO NOT have any prior knowledge in accounting, DO NOT choose blended learning mode. Some of the videos are very simple and for a starter it is very harder to catch up. Just trust me, blended learning is not for you dear.

The second thing is, my lecture (specifically L14) was full of WBB students. If you don't know what WBB is, just think of them as overpowered year 2 students from all across the globe. Not only are they elites, they also dominate all the quizzes and assignments. If you see a absurd amount of foreign students in your class then you know what to do, swap OUT of this lecture cuz its gonna be a blood bath.

Tbh if you think you are a strong student you will find it an easy course with not much new to learn but literally everyone gets full marks in everything so you better watch out for the careless mistakes.

Although I kinda caught up with everyone before finals and scored 0.33 sd above mean, I still got a C+ cuz my quizzes and assignments were miserable.
sections.workload: For a slow learning student who was definitely not meant to study business, I think having to catch up with others is already very hard. To make matters worse, Prof Chen covers one chapter a week. Each chapter has an assignment, a quiz and a group discussion. The group discussion is fine. Just open your mouth and say something. Participation is based on zoom polling.  Complete all zoom pollings in class and you will get full marks, even if you chose the wrong answer.

Homework involves 5 problem sets, and 10 smartbook exercises.  Besides the first problem set the rest are fairly short.  45 minutes should be more than enough for each.  Graded on accuracy, unlimited attempts.  The smartbook exercise is just a simple MC exercise graded on completion, designed to familiarize yourself with the content before class.  Make sure you don't miss any because they're practically free marks.

Quizzes consists of 5 quizzes, all MC, take the score of the best 4 quizzes.  Fairly simple, high mean, similar to textbook questions.

Tips for getting A:
Tang will tell you in the first class that the key to this course is practice, practice, and practice.  It is absolutely true.  Read the whole textbook (except chapter 5) and complete all textbook exercises (except chapter 1,2,5, alternate problems, and cases and projects).  Do so even if you took DSE accounting.  Quizzes have questions very similar to textbook questions so doing them will assure you score high on quizzes.  It takes about 7 hours to complete each chapter (reading + questions) without any distraction.  In reality phones are attention seekers so it will take you around 2 nights for 1 chapter.  Do them as soon as he finishes a chapter, or else you will not have enough time to finish them before quizzes.  

Textbook questions may be a bit on the easy side, but it is paramount for building good understanding, which will be crucial for the final exam.  You must fill every hole of doubt and question to score high on the finals, and the textbook questions will help you achieve that.

sections.teaching:
This Professor has several big issues in teachings.

1. His time allocation in teaching various topics is a failure. He spends about 3 weeks on the very basics of accounting. However, he rushed through the last chapters which should be considerably harder, thus will easily confuse students.

2. His teachings is very inefficient. He always introduces new things even when he is teaching the basics in the beginning, thus it takes 3 weeks for the first two topics. For example, he suddenly introduces accruals when talking about chapter 2, when accruals are supposed to be chapter 3. Also, he talks a lot on irrelevant knowledge for the exam and also repeats several times every lesson. This pointless teachings along with lame annotations made his teaching dull and pointless. In fact, I skipped most of the lessons.

3. He does not answer questions that much. Granted, he does answer questions in the lecture. However, there is one time when I send an email to him about my enquiries in chapter 12 (Cash Flow), the most recent topic, he neglected the email TWICE COMPLETELY. This is really ironic and intentional since not only I sent it twice, but I also got an immediate response right when I sent an email concerning about the exam format. This shows he is not really a reliable teacher that will answer every question.

To give him some credits, He does provide extra lesson for those new to accounting. But still, he is bad in teaching and will confuse many of the new-to-accounting students. Basically, the mean mark of the mid-term shows his teachings.

Since the final mark is still not publicized, I will only give some of my insights. The final for some reason addresses the questions topic-by-topic, starting from the last chapters to the first chapters in the exam syllabus (Note: The exam syllabus is not cumulative, from bad debts to cash flows) It is not particularly difficult but definitely harder than the Mid-term. There is much less time given to do the MCs while too much time for the LQs. In my experience, I have around 15 minutes left with the MCs but I have quite a number of them being uncertain. Test 2: 238.85 / 270 (mean: 78.38% ; StDev: 14.85%)

Terry puts all hard homework questions as test and final problems, not even changing the number. Only a very few of the questions (i.e. 2 out of 30) are new questions, but they are not hard if you understand the other questions well. sections.workload:
Extremely heavy, as I give D even I get A-

Reason for saying workload is heavy.
It is easy to see that it is heavy without comparison. 1) The total mark for all homework is 3330 and there are nearly 300 questions (including sub questions).
2) All questions are either hard or very hard. For concept questions, you must understand the whole session to get it correct. For factual questions, you at least have to read through the whole page to get the correct answer, sometimes you even need to click on the attachment or appendix to get the right answers.
3) Time is limited: Not that you are required to finish in few hours, but the total time allowed for one assignment is short. In other first year course, you have 2 weeks to finish one assignment. It is, however, not for terry's students. As he decide to put assignment after add/drop period, most assignment have to be finished in a rush. Usually 2 weeks for 2 assignment and the later one usually have 1 week only as he haven't teach. The last 3 assignments are crammed in 2 weeks. It is tough to finish it.
4) You cannot copy from internet: As aforementioned, he put homework questions in test. As a result, you need to digest it even you copy from chegg or course hero. It is more beneficial to do it yourself in my view.
5) Only 3 try. It is so different from other course and very pressured. You can understand it easily as homework accounts for 24% total mark as well as your test mark. I remember the mean for homework is 89 - 90% (not sure as he accidentally showed on lecture). You cannot form a team b/c u won't get any classmates help on zoom as he blocked the chat and there is no discussion time.
6) There are MC and long questions for homework. Long question is not easy than MC. Long questions are basically requiring you to do all the things you learnt and did in MC again. He wants to check your understanding. And some long questions are challenging that you can finish with book but not without book, which means you should revise them during the period you do homework.

Period for 1 homework:
Minimum: 5 hour
Longest: 10 hour
Average: 7 hour
(It takes so long as I learnt while doing it as mentioned, I asked my acct friends and she said she tooks 3 hours for early chapter)

Homework is one important factor that make its workload so heavy, but not the only one. Another one is practice questions.
Practice questions are very similar to homework. Terry will release homework first and then release answer for practice questions. Practice questions are after-book exercises. Those difficult after-book questions are your homework. If you want to get full in homework, you may want to do practice questions first and then use the method to check your homwork. It takes much lower time to finish practice problem as there are no MCs.
P.S. last chapter practice questions = final long questions.

Would I say workload is heavy? Definitely. But is it such bad? No. You can learn much more than other class and you can control your grade by your effort.

1) not clever but willing to paid
2) clever and willing to paid
3) want to experience the felling of an accounting student

sections.content:
Class 1: Course Overview

Pretty standard content for a foundation accounting course. I would say all of the content is useful. The content is generally easy to understand (except the Bonds part which took me two weeks to digest). Some people say that you'll have an advantage in this course if you have BAFS or high school accounting background, but I don't think it's that significant. I personally did DSE BAFS but with Sidd's teaching style and focus, many of the topics and concepts were new to me as well.
sections.teaching:
Sidd is one of the best professors I've met at UST. He always prepares real-life examples to illustrate each of the concepts, which are easy to understand. In class, he often goes through financial statements of actual (big) US companies so you get a sense of the real world. He makes sure to explain concepts in the simplest way possible, which makes his lectures extra easy to understand.

He is also very very nice and seems to have endless patience answering questions. He takes time answering even dumb questions and you can feel that he genuinely cares about his students.

However, one small problem is that his notes are not the most structured. But it's not that major as I still have no problem understanding the content, I just need some time to organize it in my mind.
sections.grading:
In terms of grading homework quizzes and exams, he is very lenient. If you look at his marking schemes, he gives partial marks even for answers that are almost completely wrong, as long as you have made some sort of attempt. It's not hard to get partial marks from him.

That being said, almost everyone gets high scores for the homework quizzes and the midterm (most people got full marks for the midterm), so it almost fully depends on your final performance. Be mentally prepared that his final is significantly harder.

Components:
15% Higher of HWQ1 or 2
15% HWQ3
30% Midterm Exam (Median: 100, Mean: ~95)
40% Final Exam (Mean: 57.24, Max: 96)

Overall I scored 96.4% which resulted in an A+
(Thank you so much Sidd for saving my cga)
sections.workload:
Very very chill I love him so much.

Firstly, he doesn't count attendance which is already a major bonus. Secondly, unlike other professors (who gives timed quizzes and homework regularly throughout the semester), we only had 3 homework quizzes and a midterm exam, all of which were take home (~30 hours to do something that can be done in 2 hours).

The final is a bit painful though. The paper is very long but you only get 3 hours to do it. He explains that this is to prevent us from cheating, which I guess is a good idea since it makes the online exam fairer. The final exam is pretty much all the workload for the entire semester.

A piece of personal advice: just make templates and excel sheets for everything in advance and that will save you a lot of time in his final.

sections.content:
The content is quite simple if you had taken BAFS in secondary school but you won't have much of a disadvantage if you didn't take accounting before since it's quite easy to catch up!

However, the final is far harder than the HW quizzes and midterm (which are quite easy since they are almost the same as the example questions)  so I strongly recommend you to look at the slides carefully even though it seems that there's not much important in some of the slides if you're a high-achiever, but some difficult questions involve points from real-life statements and articles, which I'm sure most would skip through.
sections.teaching:
Quite interesting and lively. He would use real-life examples like movies to illustrate the content and financial statements of mega-corporations, which makes it easier to understand the content. Strongly suggest you attend his lectures if possible since he occasionally talks about useful points for your assignments and tests.

His lecture notes are well-arranged so it's easy for us to find the key points of the chapter albeit there might be a lot of slides.
sections.grading:
Very lenient. He gave us 50-60% of the marks in some questions in the final we had answered incorrectly as long as we had attempted them. He also provided us answers for the HW quizzes with adequate explanations so we can understand the concepts a lot better if you didn't at first.

HW Quizzes: 30%
Midterm:30%
Final:40%
sections.workload: Quite light. We had 60 hours to finish 3 HW Quizzes ( almost 1 per month), which aren't even that long, and 72 hours to finish our midterm. But we had to finish our final within 3 hours like other courses. The workload is very manageable as long as you're not a deadline fighter.

sections.teaching:
Sidd is the best professor I have ever seen so far in HKUST.
He taught so many things other than accounting. Like he shared his own experiences and different ways of learning.

He likes to put more real-life example which makes the class less boring. You can have a basic idea of how companies in the real world is performing, why they are making different decisions and those frauds :) ... and these should be the most valuable takeaway from this course. I am very into it.

He is also lenient on grading. In homework quizzes or exams, there always will be different answer sets for the same questions. Even you cannot get the correct answer, he still gives you majority of the marks given that you have written something meaningful :D

His teaching is base on something called top-down approach. That is give the big picture first, then refines every detail (which is not suitable for me). Therefore, it is not a big problem if you don't know what he is talking about. You can ask him (he answer any kinds of questions) or wait until he gives detailed explanation.

Good English, Excellent in explaining contents. Humble and nice guy :D

sections.teaching:
Prof. TANG, Chao encourages asking questions during class by monitoring blue hands in Zoom. He also speaks clearly when in his office but I needed to listen harder during the lectures that he gave in a real classroom during mixed-mode teaching. Recommendation: get a better microphone.

The in-class exercises are very helpful as they also act as a break between listening. The Zoom polling results are also useful since I can view the percentage of classmates with my answer as well. However, only the most popular answer is highlighted in red instead of blue. Not only can I not see what I have answered, but also I cannot see the correct answer and needed to pay extra attention to the lecturer. Not sure how this can be improved.

In case you missed today's class, I want to clarify that
1) The final exam is likely more challenging than our quizzes. To help you better manage time, I put easier questions earlier and more difficult questions later.
2) It is advised that the camera should capture your hands and face during the exam. Since there is limited typing required to take the exam, the proctor may check with anyone who uses the keyboard a lot.
Best of luck and I wish you success in all your future endeavors."

Participation marks are obtained by participating in each Zoom poll each lecture. Wrong answers do not affect marks in this section, but not answering will lose marks. If 16 out of 20 polls are participated in, 4 out of 5 participation marks are obtained.

The homework consists of SmartBook assignments and Problem Sets. SmartBook assignments (0.5 points each) are for each chapter except 1, 5, and 13, where multiple-choice questions are answered repeatedly until 2 questions are answered correctly for each concept. The number of wrong answers does not affect the grade so this is where I can speedrun and find where I am not adequate quickly.

Problem Sets (4 points each) consist of 5 individual assignments where a few long fill-in-the-blank questions are answered. Originally, only 2 attempts are allowed but after the first Problem Set, it was loosened to unlimited attempts. The resulting mark of each Problem Set is the highest mark of any attempt.

I really like the quizzes where around 20 Multiple Choices are to be answered in 30 minutes with the Proctorio extension of Google Chrome to force a full screen and monitor the camera. Provided by the publisher, they allow for enough time to think about each question clearly and carefully, so I can score maximum marks each time. Moreover, he answers each question from students clearly and combined with logical slides, I am able to learn effectively. However, it messes with my dinner schedule on five Thursdays of these three months so I would like to see this changed.

Final Grade: A+ Thank you Tang Chao!!!

sections.grading:
5%的participation，【attendance≠participation】教授大人第一节课就和我们说了，你要拿分的话请说话！！！问问题！！！或者回答问题也可以呀！！！可以拿卡片！！！！写上你的大名！！！然后下课给她就好啦！！！pssssss participation最最最多可以拿到8%哦！！！！请将3%bonus一并拿到（意思就是你最高可以有103%的分数）。话说我也不知道要拿多少张卡才算满分啦所以你们就多说话吧。

40%的Final。这个是地狱啊！！！难度和前面两个根本没得比好吗！！！
我就来说一道题让你感受感受.
Bond,没有maturity date，没有issue price，没有coupon rate，没有market price，没有payment time。全部都要找出来！！！！后面那二十几个T-account把我翻得神志不清我都翻不出来答案啊！！！！！告诉我一个半年的amortization但是我不知道是effective-rate method还是straight method我怎么做嘛呜呜呜呜呜。当时我整个人是懵逼的谢谢。

不过龟还真的蛮好的。

以后大家看到她请快速飞去她的怀抱吧！！！

If you took BAFS-Acct in DSE, you will find it easy.
-Introduction and Chapter 1: Financial Statements
-Investing and Financing Decisions and the Accounting System (T-Accounts, Journal Entries)
-Operating Decisions (T-Accounts, Journal Entries)
-Adjustments, Financial Statements, and the Quality of Earnings (Creating the Balance Sheet, and Income Statement, Ratios, and Cash Flow Statement)
-Sales Revenue, Receivables, and Cash (Bad debt expense, credit sales, uncollectable receivables, aging of receivables)
-Cost of goods sold and inventory
(Methods of inventory costing)
-Property, plant, and equipment + Goodwill
(Purchase and sale of equipment, capitalization, amortization)
Operating Cycle (inventory turnover , payables outstanding, sales turnover, cash conversion)
-Time value of money
-Corporate bonds (bonds)
-Reporting liabilities (notes payable, contingent)
-Owners’ equity (Treasury stock, buybacks, preferred shares, dividends)

10% inclass participation, which is doing coursework. Pick 2 out of 3. You will have partners, but you can easily do it without the aid of any partner if you have study BAFS before.

You will learn about income statements, balance sheets, statement of cash flows, journal entries, bonds, depreciation and basic accounting policies.

sections.workload: Not heavy at all. Just two quizzes and the exam. You need to score nearly full in the two quizzes to compensate for your final. The final exam would be extremely hard, even NDS doesn't know how to do.

sections.content:
*If you haven't taken accounting before, read carefully!!

You gon get wrecked boi.

Nearly the whole class has already taken accounting somehow. You HAVE to study ahead if you don't wanna die. Learn PV and depreciation way ahead of time, and make sure you have the last 3 chapters down 100% because a lot of points in the final exam comes down to that.

The key to doing well is catching up to the class and getting ahead. Mainland chinese nibbas won't go easy on the math and since most locals already know accounting from DSEs or whatever, it's up to you to not get your ass handed to you.
sections.teaching:
Teaches very well.
One of the better lecturers for this course.

I recommend choosing this prof for lectures.
sections.grading:
Midterms - Easy af. High mean though watch out.

YO IF YOU ARE ABOUT TO PICK SZU FAN, YOU MUST KNOW THIS.

Schedule a psychiatrist for after the final exam because her exam will destroy you and give you lasting PTSD. If you thought you did well on the midterms and that you'd be fine for the finals - yeah that's where you're wrong. Study hard, do all the textbook questions and more.

Above mean on both midterms, full grades on all assignments and mean or below mean on final will give you a C.
sections.workload: Couple homework assignments, nothing much.

sections.content:
It's mainly DSE BAFS syllabus, but it's still easy even for people like me who haven't studied BAFS in secondary school.

Yet, you may get stuck in some part if you haven't fully understand the previous parts, so make sure you keep up with the learning progress, or it will be a vicious cycle.
sections.teaching: He is very enthusiastic in teaching. Some people may think he teaches too fast, but you can actually ask him to slow down a bit or ask him questions after lessons, and he is very willing to answer you.
sections.grading:
Grading is good.
Attendance: 6%
Homework: 14%
Two midterms: each 15%
Final: 50%
Midterms are easy, but the final is much more challenging and it counts a lot, so please prepare well for that.
You can easily get full mark in attendance and hw as you can miss at most two attendance and one hw.

I got full mark in hw and attendance, 96/100 in both midterms and 94/100 in final, finally got an A+

Heard people got mean and got an B, so the grading is at least satisfactory, if not very good.
sections.workload:
Very low workload.
About one hw per chapter, but it's easy and for later chapters he even gave you do solution before the deadline. But I recommend you to do it by yourself as a practice.

sections.content:

sections.teaching: Kelvin's English is acceptable with only a little bit local accent. His lecture notes do not contain many details so taking notes during lectures is important. However, Kelvin sometimes explain things in Cantonese. This is not very friendly to non-local students.
sections.grading:
Personally I don't have any opinion on the grading. Some of my friends thought the grading was quite good while some thought it harsh. But I think if you perform well in the two exams, you'll definitely get a decent grade.
Grading scheme: 10% in-class exercise (group) + 15% CSR report + 25% midterm + 50% final
My score:
in-class exercise 9.47/10 slightly above mean
CSR report 99/135 mean = 97.8(I don't know why ... I think my essay is comprehensive and profound enough. Maybe you need to consult the TA for advice)
midterm 95/100 above mean 1SD
final score was not disclosed, but should be high.
Finally got A+
I don't have any accounting background before taking the course. So you may see that it is definitely possible for you to get a good grade as long as you make efforts.
sections.workload: Light workload. The only assignment is the CSR case which you need to analyze carefully and comprehensively. But you need to do the end-chapter exercises in the textbook in order to perform well in the exams since Kelvin will not assign any homework during the semester. For the in-class exercise, plz DON'T rely on your teammates. The best way to get good marks for the in-class exercise is reviewing carefully and trying to become the leader in your group.

sections.content: Well written and presented content that is always related to the course.
sections.teaching: Teaching is quite interactive and it does not get boring. In class homework with classmates helps understand the subject better as you can get an explanation from both fellow classmates and professor.
sections.grading: Grading is done well and it is quite fair, although the essay grading was a bit harsh, but not unreasonable.
sections.workload: Workload is quite light and the only thing needed is to read the book and do all the homework. This will get you a decent grade. Follow the pace of the class and you will be just fine.

sections.content: Not difficult. Just attend every class and do some revision before final and midterm are enough to get a good grade.
sections.teaching: A little bit boring and sometimes you can get lost if not 100% focused. But the overall teaching is good.
sections.grading: Very good grading. Above mean 1.X sd in two midterms and final. Got an A at the end. One doubled size cheat sheet is allowed in the final exam. You can type the equations in case you forget.
sections.workload: Very light workload. Just finish the in-class exercises and you will be fine. And don't forget to attend the class which you are assigned to answer questions for credit.

sections.content: Content is challenging but enjoyable if you are decent with numbers.
sections.teaching: Teaching is acceptable and slides are helpful for understanding.
sections.grading: The grades are fair for an introductory course, but sufficient studying must be done outside of class. If students do more than what is assigned, they can get an A.
sections.workload: Workload is fair given the nature of the course, but studying must be done outside of the class in order to achieve a decent understanding of the material. It can be easy to excel if you put in more work than what is just assigned.

sections.content:
Basic accounting concepts
Financial statements, different assets and liabilities, etc.

Most course content are covered in HKDSE BAFS (Accounting) syllabus, so it would be easy for students who had previously studied accounting to catch up.

However, Prof. Mak used the US GAAP standard for his course. Therefore, students have to be aware of the formats and wordings, as they are slightly different from the IFAC standard.
sections.teaching:
Since the topics were categorised according to the accounts' nature, the teaching sequence was quite different from that in BAFS. Students without accounting background require greater effort to understand the content. It would be better to study the course in a comprehensive way.

In terms of the teaching quality, the lecture PowerPoints were prepared in an organised way. You need to be attentive in class to fill in some blanks and drop down the answers of the in-class discussions.

Prof. Mak was nice and patient. He explained the concepts clearly with daily examples. When someone had doubts on a certain topic, he would explain it again until everyone understands the content.
sections.grading:
Grading is fair

10% Class activities and participation
15% Case about business ethics/CSR
25% Mid-term exam
50% Final exam
Total 100%

Mid-term exam mainly examines financial statements, which is easy to handle

Final exam was not cumulative, however the questions were quite tricky and demanding

No statistics were given for the final exam

It would be fine to score a good grade if you studied hard and did adequate exercises. Students with accounting background also need practices and revision in order to score A- or above.
sections.workload:
I can say the workload is light if you compare with other courses.

No homework, only chapter exercises were given, but they were not compulsory.

No attendance would be taken, but there will be some in-class practices which counts into "Class activities and participation". You have attend those lessons and form groups with other classmates in order to get those marks.

While other professors had quizzes and regular assignments, we only had to write a CSR report before final exam (though I think there was nothing to do with the course). It would take you some time to finish the report.

sections.content: I immediately realized that a lot of the other people in class have taken accounting before, so if you haven't, you're at an immediate disadvantage. that being said, the content itself wasn't hard to absorb - it was mostly the teacher's teaching style that threw me off.
sections.teaching: szu fan has a really robotic voice that makes it really hard to focus in class. she tries to make class engaging by incorporating participation regularly and cracking a joke or two, but I can honestly say that I retained zero information during class. I legitimately tried my best to focus in the beginning, but her logic kind of bounced from place to place and her lectures became really hard to follow. I learned mostly everything from the textbook because I had no idea what was going on in class. other than that, she's a really nice lady who tries her best to help you out
sections.grading:
this is off the top of my head, I can't remember for sure if this is correct:

final exam - 40%
midterm 1 - 10%
midterm 2 - 20%
participation - 15%
in-class exercises - 15%

the two midterms, in-class exercises, and participation are basically given to you. it's super easy to score well on the two midterms, and in-class exercises are completion-based. you just have to show up to class and attempt to answer questions to get the participation points. HOWEVER, the final exam was so absurdly difficult and by no means tested the accounting we had learned in class. the entire exam was a curveball, and the people who have taken accounting already will wreck the curve for you. a cheatsheet was allowed for the final exam, but it didn't help at all. I felt like all the effort I put into the rest of the class was wasted. my entire grade was ruined by the final exam.

sections.content:
- 12 Chapters of highly relevant and useful accounting concepts that go over a lot about what it means to run a business and how to keep track of your business activities
- We used Financial Accounting - Libby, Libby, Hodge 9th Edition

Rough breakdown :
Chapter 1 : Introduction
Chapter 2 : Fundamentals of accounting
Chapter 3 : Accounting systems and how to write basic journal entries
Chapter 4 : Adjusting entries, Balance Sheet, Income Statement
(we skipped chapter 5)
Chapter 6 : Accounts Receivables, Bad debts, Allowance for doubtful accounts (we skipped the second half of the chapter)
Chapter 7 : Inventory, FIFO, LIFO (we skipped the latter part of the chapter)
Chapter 8 : Property, Plant, Equipment (we skipped a lot of the content in this chapter)
Chapter 9 : Liabilities (we mostly skimmed this chapter, and focused on the present value of money)
Chapter 10 : Bonds and Accounting for bonds purchased at premium and at discount
Chapter 11 : Stockholders' Equity
Chapter 12 : Statement of Cash Flows
Chapter 13 : Analyzing financial statements (this was a bonus chapter that he discussed for fun; not tested)
sections.teaching:
- Fun, engaging, and very detailed teaching
- The professor is very willing to answer questions in class and is quite helpful as well, as he is willing to conduct additional study sessions and consultation sessions after the midterms and before the finals
- He provides very detailed study guides which were very useful for the midterms, but not so much for the finals which was a bit of a surprise at the end

- Unfortunately, it is not very easy to contact the professor outside class; he does not always respond to emails and has said in his course outline that he will not answer questions asked via email :/
- Also, the canvas discussion boards are empty
- The teaching pace is quite fast too; might be a bit challenging if you are not a fast learner or if you are sleepy during class (like me)
sections.grading:
I was worried that my grades would not be so ideal due to the steep curve, but actually, it is possible to score A range even when you make several mistakes in the midterms and the finals

2 Midterms (15% each)
- Not too difficult, imo, just be careful when reading the question and do the journal entries carefully (e.g. remember to write the date)

1 Final (50%)
- Rather challenging
- some multiple choice questions asked about things mentioned briefly only
- the last part asks several questions based on tons of T accounts - have a good eye for dates and practice working backwards

Attendance and Classroom performance (6%)
- he likes checking attendance using in-class quizzes, so try and attend the lectures

Assignments (14%)
- quite easy to get high marks here, especially since he grades assignments by effort, not accuracy
sections.workload:
Roughly one assignment per chapter, not too difficult; they serve as good practice too

2 Midterms
1 Final

I did not spend much time on this course because my other courses ate up so much of my time; still managed to do well though

sections.content:
1. Basic accounting entry
Need to understand different accounts. Note that some terms or accounts are different from the BAFS in secondary school.

Professor goes through all basic entry skills in just two weeks, so it may be challenging for students without accounting background.

2. Sales and bad debt
Not difficult to understand.

3. Liabilities: Bonds and present value
Pay attention to professor as this part involves a bit complex calculation. Remember to consider the present value when calculating the net value of bonds.

4. Shareholders' equity
Just something about shares. Not difficult.

5. Cash flow
Remember to understand the principle of indirect method. Especially pay attention when calculating operating cash flow as you need to minus the financing and investing cash flow.
sections.teaching:
A bit too fast for students without accounting background knowledge. I cannot understand what she taught at the beginning few lectures.

However, she is very patient and is willing to answer questions from students. All questions must be asked face-to-face or through Canvas discussion board. That's a great thing as you can know what others are asking

Read the questions in discussion board before exams as this may help you.
sections.grading:
My score and grade:
In class exercise: 24/24
Attendance: 6/6
Quiz 1: 26.5/32 [Mean 28]
Quiz 2: 79/85 [Mean 71]
Final exam: 104/150 [Mean 75]
Grade: A-

In class exercise 24%
Remember to finish 8 out of 10 in Class Exercise. Professor would discuss the answer in class, but you need to type of write the answer and upload your answer (no need to be correct) to Canvas.

Answering questions + attendance 6%
Professor would tell you when she take your attendance. Just attend lecture that day, answer questions to get full credit (no need to be correct).

Quiz 1 10%
Quiz 2 20%
Two quizzes are much easier than the final exam, but the mean is extraordinarily high. No cheat sheet. Make sure to revise and be careful.

Final exam 40%
Although more difficult than quizzes, it's not that difficult compared with last few years. One cheat sheet (A4 both side) is allowed so don't recite too much. She tend to ask more practical questions, so do more exercise instead.

She divides the final exam to 3 parts: Basic questions (~30%), Intermediate questions (~50%) and challenging questions (~20%). Those challenging questions are all about effects of accounts when mistakes are made, which indeed not that scary.
sections.workload:
In class exercise sometimes require quite a long time to write although she would discuss the answer (especially preparing all T-accounts), so don't wait until the last minute to do if you want.

However you can just write something and submit and still get full credit :) Make sure to understand the in class exercise as similar questions would appear in quizzes and exam

No projects.

sections.content: Content is alright, he expects you to have prior knowledge of the course, but even if you don't, going through the textbook and understanding it is good enough, until the final exam, which is absolutely dreadful.
sections.teaching: He is a nice guy, entertaining, will try to keep your interest levels high, remembers everyone's names, which is really nice. However, since he expects you to know the course, it always feels like there is no room for error. It is hard to understand him sometimes, especially if you have no prior accounting background.
sections.grading: His examination system is rather different. He will have 2 quizzes and 1 midterm, homework, attendance and the final exam. It is relatively easy to score a high mark in the quizzes, midterm and homework, however, even if you get above the mean in most of his tests, it doesn't mean that you'll get a good grade. The final pulls everyone down, and the final is really hard, most of it, you can't understand, even if you go through the textbook thoroughly.
sections.workload: Workload is alright. There will be times when it gets a bit stressful, but as long as you keep yourself updated every week or two, it should be okay. Initially, it seems to be overwhelming, since he expects a certain amount of knowledge and does reduce your confidence levels, which isn't the best thing considering you're doing accounting for the first time in your life.

He supposes us knowing everything, thus rarely do live demonstration on perplexing problems. What he does every lecture is just explaining concepts and definitions that are not very important and share his own experience. After that he directly asks students to do his assigned practices from textbook and starts reading out students' name one by one to take attendance. I have sit for Chen Szu Fan's lecture and I found her teaching is rather easier to follow for beginners. Gerry's unappealing lecture could be reflected by the attendance rate. I realised that after midterm, the attendance soon dropped to 60-70% though attendance is 10% of the course grade. Yet, the good thing is Gerry will provide full solution for his suggested practices of every chapter. After all, it is better to count on your hard-work instead of professor's teaching to earn your course grade.

To me, the grading is fine. I am a Business minor student (from Science School) with no prior high school background. Some people said it is hard to survive Gerry's Accounting course if you only are a beginner (because of the terrible teaching), making it impossible to get a C grade or above. This is not the real case if you are hard working enough and using the right way for studying, understanding every concept thoroughly. That is why after my disastrous performance in Quiz 1, my results for other tests improved drastically. Unfortunately, I have no time for revision of the final exam (my Organic Chemistry exam was on the same morning!!!) -- I only studied for 4 hours right before the final exam!!! It is great that Gerry did not give me a C grade. If I were in Chen Szu Fan's class, I would probably end up a D grade!!!
sections.workload:
If you are not aiming high and you already have some Accounting background, I would say the workload is low. Basically when grading the homework, the TA wouldn't care about the correctness of your answers and figures. As long as you finish all the assigned problems, the TA would give you full score. All the tests are not difficult as well when compared to other professors'. However, such easiness implies difficulty to achieve good grade. If you aim high, it is better to read through the textbook carefully and finish every single problem, which is rather time-consuming. Remember, practice makes perfect!

There are several points that you need to pay attention with. For the two quizzes, rather than being application-oriented, Gerry also covers some subtle concepts from notes and textbooks that students normally skip. Only being able to do calculations is likely to cause you below mean (or at most slightly above mean). Don't think quizzes with MCQs only are that easy!

For the midterm exam, as long as you can do all calculations without mistakes, you will be fine. For the final exam, although only the last five chapters are covered, please don't forget the fundamental concepts taught in the first half of the course. Don't be satisfied with the illusion that you are able to complete all the practice exercises on textbook. Otherwise you will cry in the final exam! Plus, unlike the midterm, there are several questions that require you to give definitions, provide examples, and do comparisons. I guess most students won't pay much attention to such details. I guess Gerry use these to differentiate between A+ and A grade students.
